TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index was up more than 300 points in late-morning trading, helped by strength in the telecom, industrial and financial sectors, while U.S. stock markets were mixed.

The S&P/TSX composite index was up 313.44 points at 35,897.90.

The Canadian dollar traded for 70.45 cents US compared with 70.11 cents US on Wednesday.

items._ogDesc: The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen restrictions that violated the Competition Act.
items.body:
The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen data-sharing restrictions that violated the Competition Act.

The watchdog says the Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers and its subsidiary, Société Centris, broke abuse of dominance rules by refusing to provide its members with a real estate data feed, while also restricting how such data could be used.

The bureau says lack of access to that data was likely meant to “impede innovation and limit competition in the real estate brokerage services market.”

  • Most recent real estate news from BNNBloomberg.ca

As part of a consent agreement reached with the association, it will now provide its members with a real estate data feed containing information about sale prices, listing history and property characteristics.

Pierre-Olivier Simard, president of the QPAREB board of directors, says in a statement that the solution is “tailored to the Quebec reality,” given that Quebec’s laws are more restrictive than those in the rest of Canada when it comes to the protection of personal information.

The bureau launched its investigation into QPAREB’s data-sharing practices in 2023 after a previous case against the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, in which the watchdog challenged rules that prevented brokers in that region from sharing certain real estate data with their clients through secure online platforms.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: AI stocks keep falling, but the rest of the market is supporting Wall Street
items.description: More drops for artificial-intelligence stocks are hitting Wall Street Thursday, but gains for the rest of the market are keeping U.S. indexes near their records.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Options trader Anthony Spina works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: More drops for artificial-intelligence stocks are hitting Wall Street Thursday, but gains for the rest of the market are keeping U.S. indexes near their records.
items.body:
More drops for artificial-intelligence stocks are hitting Wall Street Thursday, but gains for the rest of the market are keeping U.S. indexes near their records.

The S&P 500 was virtually unchanged in midday trading after erasing an early loss. The weakness for AI stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down 0.4 per cent, but the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 440 points, or 0.9 per cent, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time as the majority of U.S stocks climbed.

The sharp drops for AI stocks began on Wall Street Wednesday and then whipped around the world to send South Korea’s Kospi down 7.6 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 4.9 per cent before returning to the United States.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

It’s their latest stunning swing after they led the market for years. Companies are pouring money into AI in hopes of bigger profits and improved productivity. But data centers and AI chips cost money, and many companies have been borrowing the cash to get them.

Now, after yields in bond markets worldwide hit their highest levels in years, worries are rising about how resilient that boom in spending can be. Many AI-related companies have already taken on debt to build out their aspirations, and stocks are struggling under the debt loads.

CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, fell 5.2 per cent a day after tumbling 15.5 per cent. It said in the summer that it had US$4.41 billion in principal payments to make on its debt over the second half of this year and another US$6.18 billion in 2027. It had more than US$5.5 billion in cash, as of June 30.

High yields in the bond market also generally make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks, particularly those seen as the most expensive.

Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the AI boom to become Wall Street’s most valuable company, fell 1.9 per cent and was the day’s heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It came into the day with a nearly 1,415 per cent gain since the end of 2022.

The losses came despite a strong profit report from a bellwether of the AI industry. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported a profit for the latest quarter that topped analysts’ high expectations, and Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said it expects strong demand to continue in the final three months of 2026.

Its stock that trades in the United States fell 2.6 per cent.

A day earlier, another major player in the AI industry likewise delivered a strong profit report that failed to stir excitement for the industry. Christophe Fouquet, the CEO of ASML in the Netherlands, said demand has been so strong because of AI that some customers are talking about placing orders for as far out as 2029 or even 2030.

Outside of AI, stocks were more resilient.

Marsh & McLennan climbed 6.4 per cent to help lead the market after the insurance and professional services firm reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company, which updated its brand name to Marsh early this year, also delivered higher revenue than expected.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Expectations are high for profits at all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. Companies will need to surpass them to keep driving their stock prices to more records when high inflation and many other worries are weighing on Wall Street.

Seven out of every 10 stocks within the S&P 500 rose. But because AI stocks have become so big in market value, their stock movements have more effect on the index and can drown out the rest of the market.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market on Thursday, which means investors are willing to pay higher prices to buy U.S. government bonds. Treasurys have a reputation as a safer investment, one with less risk of the borrower going bankrupt, and investors often flock to them when feeling nervous.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.07 per cent from 5.19 per cent late Wednesday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The drop in yields came even though another report signaled inflation has worsened by even more in the United States than economists expected.

Several reports on the U.S. economy also came in stronger than economists expected, which typically push yields upward. One report said U.S. retailers made more money last month than economists expected, while another said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than expected.

In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s loss was the headliner. Its Kospi index is dominated by two chip companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and it fell to its worst day since July. It has dropped 39 per cent since setting a record in June.

Indexes were stronger in Europe, and London’s FTSE 100 rallied 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
items.body:
TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

  • Latest updates on company news here

SeatGeek Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties.

Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties.

However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000. 

“We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said.

SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays.

The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows.

After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences.

A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations.

The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket.

To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Nobody likes taking a loss when selling stocks, but experts say now is the time to look at your portfolio and see if there are any investments that haven’t worked out as you hoped that might help you reduce your tax bill.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Nobody likes taking a loss when selling stocks, but experts say now is the time to look at your portfolio and see if there are any investments that haven’t worked out as you hoped that might help you reduce your tax bill.

Reviewing your portfolio and taking a look at what gains you’ve seen and how you might be able to offset them with any losses should be part of your year-end tax planning.

Kris Kibler, tax planning lead at Wealthsimple, says if you are selling shares at a loss, that deficit can be used to offset capital gains on better performing stocks, reducing the amount of tax you will owe.

He explained that if you bought shares for $10,000 and later sold them for $7,000, the $3,000 capital loss could be deducted against capital gains.

That deduction will reduce the amount of tax you might owe when you file your return next year.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Kibler says it is important that tax-loss selling isn’t done in a vacuum.

“You don’t necessarily engage in tax-loss harvesting or tax-loss selling in order to just take advantage of the tax implication with disregard for the investment portfolio overall,” he says.

“This always wants to be kind of done in tandem with your overall investment and financial plan as a whole.”

It is also important to ensure you don’t run afoul of the rules governing what losses you can claim.

Tax-loss selling only applies to taxable or non-registered accounts. Losses in accounts such as your TFSA, RRSP or RESP cannot be used to offset your taxable gains outside those accounts.

The losses can only be used to offset any taxable capital gains you have. They can’t be deducted from your regular income. If you don’t have any capital gains to offset this year, your losses can be used to reduce your taxable capital gains going back three years or you can carry the losses forward to use in future years.

CRA also doesn’t allow what is referred to as a superficial loss, which prevents you from claiming the loss if the same or identical security is repurchased within a 61-day window starting 30 calendar days before the sale and extending 30 days after the sale.

The superficial loss rules don’t just apply to your account, but also extend to your spouse or common-law partner, corporations you or your spouse control, or what the CRA calls an affiliated person.

“What the CRA doesn’t want you to do is get the advantages of the tax-loss harvesting or tax-loss selling strategy in order to get the benefit and then purchase the exact same securities again and continue in the same portfolio,” Kibler said.

Julie Petrera, director of financial planning at Edward Jones, says it is important to remember that tax-loss selling is not an investment strategy.

“It should support your long-term goals but not drive your long-term investing goal,” she said.

“I wouldn’t make decisions on what I’m holding in my portfolio just for short-term tax reasons.”

Petrera said losses are part of investing at times, but tax-loss selling is the “silver lining” when you have securities that have gone down.

“While you have lost money on that security or on that investment, the money that you’ve lost could be made up for in tax savings applied to another investment,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Craig Wong, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The federal government plans to spend $430 million over the next five years to help unions train a new generation of skilled trades workers.
items.body:
The federal government plans to spend $430 million over the next five years to help unions train a new generation of workers in the skilled trades.

John Zerucelli, secretary of state for labour, announced Thursday that Ottawa is opening applications for access to the new pool of funding, most which comes from an expansion to the Union Training and Innovation Program launched in 2017.

The federal government says in a news release that unions and training providers will be able to apply for extra capital to expand their training facilities and other infrastructure. Expressions of interest are open until Nov. 12 and the government is looking for shovel-ready projects that can begin next spring.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The government is also now accepting ongoing applications to offset the cost of equipment for training and is temporarily boosting the share it covers to 70 per cent, up from 50 per cent previously.

A third application stream will fund unions’ proposals for innovative ways to attract, recruit and support trainees before and throughout the apprenticeship process. Organizations with pitches can submit a proposal to the government by Dec. 17.

Nearly half of today’s funding announcement is accounted for in a previous Liberal government pledge to spend $8 billion to recruit and train up to 100,000 new skilled trades workers over the next five years.

The Liberal government has focused on the skilled trades over the past year as it pursues an ambitious infrastructure agenda.

Zerucelli said in a media statement that Canada needs more workers to build homes, infrastructure and major projects to boost the economy.

“That’s why we’re investing in apprenticeship training facilities, modern equipment, and new approaches to training, giving more Canadians the opportunity to learn a trade, develop their skills and build Canada’s future,” he said.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: WEF could appoint Lagarde as early as November, Reuters sources say
items.description: The World Economic Forum could appoint Christine Lagarde as its next chair as soon as next month, four people close to the organization told Reuters, meaning she would step down early as European Central Bank chief and trigger a wider reshuffle at the top of the ECB.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde briefs the media during a press conference at the bank's headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany, Thursday, Sept. 11, 2025. (AP Photo/Michael Probst, File)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The World Economic Forum could appoint Christine Lagarde as its next chair as soon as next month, four people close to the organization told Reuters, meaning she would step down early as European Central Bank chief and trigger a wider reshuffle at the top of the ECB.
items.body:
ZURICH/BANGKOK -- The World Economic Forum could appoint Christine Lagarde as its next chair as soon as next month, four people close to the organization told Reuters, meaning she would step down early as European Central Bank chief and trigger a wider reshuffle at the top of the ECB.

Lagarde’s ECB term is scheduled to end in October 2027. Leaving early would give European Union leaders a chance to pick a new ECB President before France’s spring presidential election, which opinion polls suggest the far-right could win, and could pave the way for a deal involving two other senior ECB roles.

The WEF’s Board of Trustees, which includes Lagarde herself, will meet on November 2 and could elect her as its next chair, said the people close to the organization, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

  • Latest updates on international news here

No final decision has been taken yet, they said.

Two of the people said the board could instead use the meeting to set a date for a vote that would enable Lagarde to appear as the designated chair when the WEF’s annual meeting takes place in January in Davos, where political and business leaders gather to discuss global economic and financial issues.

They cautioned that Lagarde’s election was not certain but said the 70-year-old former French finance minister had broad support from the board, which lists 27 members on its website.

The ECB declined to comment.

The WEF didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Finding successor before French elections

Either timetable would leave enough time for a new ECB President to clear all the formal hurdles that come with EU appointments well before the end of French President Emmanuel Macron’s term in May.

Lagarde’s desire to give Macron a say on her successor was one factor in the timing, a fifth person said. There is concern in European political circles that negotiations over who takes over from her could become more difficult if far-right leader Marine Le Pen were to win the French presidency.

Based in Geneva, the WEF board is currently co-chaired by BlackRock Chief Executive Larry Fink and Roche Vice Chairman Andre Hoffmann, who assumed the role after founder Klaus Schwab stepped down last year.

The board also includes public-sector figures such as International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and Jordan’s Queen Rania and leading business chiefs like Salesforce’s Marc Benioff and Siemens’ Jim Hagemann Snabe.

Lagarde, who is attending the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, has said she will remain at the ECB until next year but has stopped short of committing to remain until her term formally ends in October.

Her exit would open a second vacancy on the ECB’s six-member Executive Board after Isabel Schnabel’s resignation last month. Chief Economist Philip Lane is meanwhile due to step down in May.

EU officials say the three appointments could be agreed as part of a package deal among member states.

The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners for the presidency, while France is understood to be targeting the chief economist’s post.

Germany plans to put forward a candidate to replace Schnabel, who heads the ECB’s market operations, the people said.

By Dave Graham and Francesco Canepa

(Additional reporting by John Revill and Oliver Hirt in Zurich and Olivia Le Poidevin in Geneva; Editing by Mark John and Hugh Lawson)

items.body:
OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says total manufacturing sales rose 1.5 per cent to $79.9 billion in August, helped by strength in the primary metal and chemical subsectors.

Sales in the primary metal subsector gained 14.0 per cent to hit a record $7.6 billion in August, helped by higher sales volumes and prices, while the chemical subsector increased 4.4 per cent to $6.2 billion.

Transportation equipment sales fell 2.6 per cent to $12.0 billion.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

In constant dollars, total manufacturing sales were unchanged in August.

In a separate report, Statistics Canada says wholesale sales, excluding petroleum, petroleum products, and other hydrocarbons as well as oilseed and grain, fell 1.6 per cent to $91.6 billion in August.

In volume terms, wholesale sales, excluding the same categories, fell 1.8 per cent.

Statistics Canada has started including oilseed and grain as well as the petroleum and petroleum products subsector as part of wholesale trade but is excluding the data from its monthly analysis until there is enough historical data for comparison.

items.title: Feds looking to build $1.5 billion data centre in Ottawa area
items.description: The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.
items._ogDesc: The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.
items.body:
The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.

Defence Construction Canada issued an advance procurement notice for the data centre last week, saying it is informing “design-builders of an upcoming contract located” in the Ottawa area.

The estimated cost of the project is $1.5 billion to $1.8 billion, with the tender expected to be issued in 2027.

“To increase its capacity in supporting the mid to long-term objectives related to operations, security, and technology modernization, the Government of Canada is planning to design and construction a data centre facility within the national capital region,” said the notice issued on the federal government’s website.

“This data center of 60 MW will enable the onboarding of next-generation capabilities with tailored mechanical and electrical configurations to meet distinct technology requirements throughout the facility.”

The government’s proposed data centre facility would include a “small office space and a shipping and receiving area,” according to the notice. It also notes the federal government has not approved proceeding with the new data centre at this time.

In August, Ottawa city council passed a motion directing city staff to develop a framework for assessing data centre proposals. The study will look at assessing data centres based on their size and impact, including environmental and industrial standards, community benefits and possible amendments to the official plan.

Hydro Ottawa’s CEO Bryce Conrad told council in June that the utility had received 34 requests in the past two years for “large load customers,” which would require nearly 90 per cent of the average amount of power used by the City of Ottawa in 2025.

“These are prospective customers who need a significant amount of electricity, think of government, national defence, hospitals, university campuses, and yes, data centres,” Conrad said, noting data centres accounted for 653 megawatts of the 1,075-megawatts requested to Hydro Ottawa.

“It’s no secret that there’s a lot of tension these days around data centres, AI technologies, and their tremendous appetite for power.”

During an interview with Newstalk 580 CFRA in August, Conrad said Hydro Ottawa is working to build capacity to meet the demand for data centres and large-load customers.

“We’re probably being asked to build in the next two or three years that which has taken us about 110 years to build.”

items.title: Royal LePage: trade tensions stall Canada’s fall housing market
items.description: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.content: <p>Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/073/0388_639276754438511603.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.body:
Canada’s housing market stalled in the third quarter of 2026 as new US tariffs and the prospect of higher mortgage rates kept buyers sidelined, according to the Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast.

The national aggregate home price slipped 0.8% year over year to $810,000 and fell 0.6% from the second quarter. Royal LePage now forecasts a 1.0% annual gain in the fourth quarter, down from the 2.0% it projected in its second-quarter house price survey.

Greater Toronto Area prices fell 3.7% to $1,073,100, while Greater Vancouver dropped 4.0% to $1,148,100.

Greater Montreal bucked the trend with a 2.9% gain to $653,700, and Prairie markets held steadier.

The trade dispute escalated after talks collapsed on Aug. 21 and Washington imposed a 50% tariff on a wide range of Canadian goods a day later.

“For many buyers, the hesitation is less about what they can afford today than how secure they feel about tomorrow,” said Phil Soper, president and CEO of Royal LePage.

“Buyers have more negotiating power, but little control over the forces shaping their confidence.”

BMO senior economist Sal Guatieri flagged the same risk in April.

“Unfortunately, it’s the economic uncertainty – both related to the trade war and the Iran war – that will likely keep a lot of buyers, especially first-time buyers, on the sidelines,” he said.

Royal LePage home prices by market, Q3 2026

Aggregate and median prices, with Royal LePage’s year-end forecast

*Forecast change in aggregate price, Q4 2026 vs. Q4 2025. Prices include resale and new build. Negative figures shown in red.
Source: Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast, Q3 2026 (released Oct. 15, 2026); price data from RPS Real Property Solutions

Mortgage rate jitters fail to pull buyers forward

The Bank of Canada has held its overnight rate at 2.25% for a year, with announcements due Oct. 28 and Dec. 9. Soper expects a hold through 2026 and a hike in early 2027, though a growing number of forecasters are calling for an October rate hike.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, is among those expecting an earlier move.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” he shared during MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal. Armstrong argued the risk is manageable.

“I think everyone got really worried about the renewal cliff. So they got really good at preparing for it. And I think that preparation has taken the noise out of it,” he said.

“We’re in normal rates today. We’re not in obscenely high rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn’t exist to the extreme, but it’s something we need to be aware of.”

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What brokers are seeing on the ground

For buyers who do act, leverage has shifted. “Conditions of finance are back in. Home inspections, everything, you name it. Water testing. We have price reductions,” said Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ont., who spoke at MortgageFest.

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said brokers must understand the macro picture without guessing at it.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” she explained during the mortgage event.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, sees a slow climb rather than a rebound and also shared his thoughts during MortgageFest Canada.

“I’d like to be optimistic. I think we’re facing the reality that with the geopolitical climate and everything that’s happening here, our mortgage industry is probably not ready to rebound. We are seeing slight growth in originations, we’re seeing slight growth in mortgage balances – a lot more on the refi side,” he said.

Soper remains measured. “Canada’s housing market is on a detour, not a derailment,” he said.

items.title: Trump says Canada will ‘end up being the 51st state’
items.description: Donald Trump told a crowd of supporters that Canada will "end up being the 51st state" as he expressed a series of longstanding grievances the United States has with its northern neighbour.

items._ogDesc: Donald Trump told a crowd of supporters that Canada will "end up being the 51st state" as he expressed a series of longstanding grievances the United States has with its northern neighbour.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump told a crowd of supporters that Canada will “end up being the 51st state” as he listed a series of longstanding grievances the United States has with its northern neighbour.

“Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not anymore. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town,” he said during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., on Wednesday.

Trump brought up Canadian tariffs on milk, car companies moving their factories to the U.S. and renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

According to the U.S. president, Canada “ripped off” the U.S. through tariffs on “anything past two bottles (of milk).”

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” Trump said. “We don’t need them, but they need us.”

The U.S. president then asked why the U.S. should be losing billions of dollars “to support a country that isn’t one of us?”

“They’ll be doing something just like Greenland,” he said, adding that it “just adds to our beautiful plate,” referring to the U.S.

“Our plate’s getting larger all the time.”

Foreign meddling

Trump made the comments on the same day Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to “political interference” in close races ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.

Hoekstra pointed to comments made by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who said in August that Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are designed to target specific U.S. states.

“It appears that some of this, from our perspective, in the way we view our elections, could be inferred to be election interference,” the ambassador said in an interview on “The Really Big Show” podcast.

One of those close races is in Michigan, where Democrats have tied Trump’s tariff policies to the higher cost of living facing Americans.

Meanwhile, Trump has commented on the elections of several countries throughout his second term in office. Last weekend, he said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the United States.

The president also advocated for Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s elections earlier this month, and endorsed former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban ahead of his election loss in April.

‘Never the 51st state’

Following the announcement of Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs on American goods in September, B.C. Premier David Eby announced that the province will install new signs at the U.S. border crossings declaring the province “never the 51st state.”

U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick targeted Ontario in “51st state” remarks last month, saying the province would be the “last out of our 51st states.” The comment was a response to Prime Minister Mark Carney, who called on the Trump administration to “start being serious” about trade negotiations.

In June, when Canada slipped into what some economists said met the definition of a technical recession, Trump revived his call to the country to become the “51st state” on social media. The move drew sharp criticism from officials from across Canada.

Soon after, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the president was “back on his high horse” and that Canada’s sovereignty is not for sale.

“I can tell President Trump that will never, ever happen.”

With files from CTV News’ Codi Wilson, Todd Coyne

items.title: How credit unions are navigating a turbulent 2026 market
items.description: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.content: <p>CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639276728476168839.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.body:
Canada’s current housing market is moribund, according to a leading community lending chief executive officer. And that means credit unions are navigating a difficult balancing act: maintaining volumes without taking on undue risk in a market where prices are still falling.

Fausto Gaudio, president and chief executive officer of the Toronto-headquartered IC Savings, described the current market as one where activity was barely getting off the ground. “It’s very, very soft,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “Softer than it was last year – and last year was also a very soft year in terms of trades and prices declining as well.”

That marks one of the biggest obstacles facing credit unions and other lenders. Maintaining asset size is no easy feat, but loosening credit standards to bring more business in isn’t always the best idea either as values continue to slide.

“Top of mind is that there just isn’t enough volume,” Gaudio said. “It’s very, very difficult… to maintain asset size, because unless we expand our risk tolerance and do mortgages at a higher loan-to-value at a time when prices are declining. That’s a real challenge, especially for small boutique lenders.”

Gaudio said IC Savings has opted to hold its position rather than chase volume, steering clear of high-LTV lending. “We do very few mortgages at the 80% loan-to-value,” he said. “And so we don’t seem to have a lot of the problems that the big banks have in terms of defaults and powers of sale today.”

But there’s also opportunity in the market, not least in serving borrowers who fall outside standard bank approval criteria. Tighter lending standards among Canada’s banking giants mean borrowers often don’t qualify in the current market not because of recklessness, but rather circumstance.

When dealing with those customers, understanding the story – and the “why” of how their current situation developed – is crucial, according to Gaudio.

“With somebody that might have had a difficulty – having gone through a health problem, a period of unemployment, a marital breakup – we’re much more attentive to those human stories and try to resolve their problems,” he said.

“When a borrower is coming out of a life experience and a setback, we’re much more willing to try to resolve their issue – but at the same time, they need to have some equity to offset that risk.”

Reverse mortgages: Will their popularity grow in the credit union space?

Gaudio said IC Savings has developed a new term reverse mortgage, a fixed-period alternative to the traditional lifetime arrangement, aimed at homeowners who want to access equity but have a clear exit plan within a few years.

The product, he said, is for “someone that wants to live in their house another three or possibly five years, but then they have a plan – to move back to Northern Ontario or the East Coast where they had family or grandkids – but they don’t want to commit to a reverse mortgage for life.”

2027 outlook for wider market remains unclear

Gaudio sees the current housing market sluggishness as a product of rampant unaffordability rather than the geopolitical headwinds hovering over the Canadian economy.

Trade turmoil and rising oil prices, he said, have less impact of the housing market than the fact that prices have skyrocketed over the past decade, and remain elevated in many regions despite the years-long cooldown.

It remains unclear whether the broader market will normalize quickly enough to ease volume pressure on boutique lenders heading into 2027, but with borrower stress likely to continue rising, he emphasized the importance of brokers and agents telling their customer’s story in as much detail as possible to boost their chances of getting a deal through.

“I believe the brokers that deal with us know us as that type of lender,” he said.

items.title: Housing coalition outlines four demands ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items._ogDesc: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items.body:
Market-rate developers and non-profit housing providers are joining forces to urge B.C.’s political parties to reduce the cost of building homes, warning that rising expenses and policy uncertainty are leaving projects stalled.

The Urban Development Institute (UDI), B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA) and Co-operative Housing Federation of B.C. (CHF BC) on Tuesday called on all parties to commit to four measures aimed at making housing development more financially viable.

The groups said the cost of building and financing homes in B.C. has exceeded what many buyers can afford and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters, resulting in projects failing to get off the drawing board.

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” said Mike Drummond, CEO of UDI, in a statement.

The groups are asking the next provincial government to restore planned investments in non-profit, co-operative and Indigenous housing, allowing more than 5,000 affordable rental homes that were deferred following $1.4 billion in recent budget cuts to proceed.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association.

“The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

The coalition also called on the government to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to “continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market.”

In addition, the groups urged the next government to finalize a federal-provincial agreement to reduce development cost charges and fund infrastructure needed to support new housing within 90 days of forming government.

The federal and provincial governments announced a 10-year partnership in June under which they would each contribute nearly $1.6 billion to reduce development charges for multi-unit housing by up to 50 per cent in priority communities and fund infrastructure.

“The details were not finalized before the election was called, so builders cannot price it into projects and municipalities cannot act on it,” said the coalition in a statement Tuesday.

Lastly, the groups called for a federal GST exemption on new homes for all eligible buyers rather than limiting relief to first-time purchasers. They pointed to Ontario’s expanded HST rebate program, announced in March, which temporarily eliminated the 13 per cent HST on eligible buyers of new homes valued at $1 million or less.

“The commitments made in 2024 need to translate into homes on the ground,” said Margaret Pfoh, CEO of the Aboriginal Housing Management Association, in a statement.

items._ogDesc: Canadians expect to buy their first home at 41, while nearly half of homeowners can’t afford their next move, an RBC poll finds.
items.body:
Canada’s housing ladder isn’t just hard to get on—nearly half of owners can’t afford to get off the first rung. RBC’s 2026 Home Ownership Poll looked at home buying expectations and financial constraints. The poll shows first-time buyers are getting older, and fewer owners can afford to upgrade. Meanwhile, the Bank of Mom and Dad is expanding its territory—literally, as multi-generational living returns.

Canada’s First-Time Buyers Expect To Buy Their First Home At 41

Canada’s first-time buyers will be on the back half of life’s golf course before they get into the market. Aspiring first-time owners plan to buy at 41 years old on average, 12 years later than current owners. That may be an optimistic number, as nearly half of them were unsure when they would be able to buy a home.

Becoming a homeowner is much harder than it was for past generations, said most (74%) of non-owners. Over 3 in 4 (77%) believe buying is harder than it was in the past, and 60% say traditional buyer advice is no longer true. Existing homeowners are likely to agree with that last point.

Canadian Homeowners Can’t Afford To Upgrade Their Starter Home

High home prices don’t just impact first-time buyers, it causes buyer gridlock. Modern housing markets are built around the concept of a property ladder. Homebuyers progressively move up the ladder, upgrading as they build equity. That process has been breaking down, as fewer people can afford to upgrade.

Nearly half (46%) of current owners want a larger or different home, but say it’s not financially realistic. Most (52%) say moving up from their first home is harder than expected, a problem the whole industry is about to feel. If existing starter home owners can’t buy the next rung, those sellers face reduced liquidity. At the same time, there are fewer starter homes for buyers to get onto the property ladder in the first place.

Aspiring first-time homebuyers are taking note and skipping the ladder. The survey found 74% are looking for a long-term home instead of a starter. Starting ownership 12 years later than average means very different property needs. Delaying their buy until the age of their peak earnings growth can help them afford to skip the starter. It also means starter homeowners will see their liquidity turn into their competition.

RBC senior mortgage specialist Brad Evjen suggests this may not always be the best strategy. “Buying a home you can stay in longer usually means stretching your budget further, so the math has to work in both directions,” he notes. He prefers to walk clients through monthly payments against what moving up in five years would cost.

Usually, the down payment problem is a bigger hurdle than the monthly payment. First-time buyers are increasingly tapping the Bank of Mom and Dad. However, not everyone’s parents are rich—some are actually looking for help with their own cost of living.

Multi-Generational Households Return With High Home Prices

Canada’s lack of affordability may soon reverse nuclear households to their pre-war roots. The survey found that 57% of prospective first-time buyers would consider multi-generational living—parents living with their adult children. However, it’s not just a first-time buyer thing—most buyers (53%), including those who currently own, would consider multi-generational living. Nearly half (44%) of all respondents, including those not in the housing market at all, would also consider the option.

Only a few years ago, it became normal for parents to help with a down payment. Now 29% of prospective first-time buyers say multi-generational buying is more a necessity than a choice. A problem that parents are receptive to—35% of homeowners say they’re prepared to sell and jointly buy with their kids to help them enter the market.

Canada’s housing ladder is difficult to enter—and getting onto it doesn’t guarantee you can climb it. Those looking to enter the market can’t do so until much later in life. At the same time, those who own are increasingly struggling to upgrade from their starter. Helping to bridge the gap are families pooling resources to buy what was considered normal for the last three generations.

items.title: OCC debanking report names TD Bank, BMO in major US probe
items.description: US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers
items.content: <p>US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276064635054189.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers
items.body:
Two of Canada’s largest lenders, Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD) and the Bank of Montreal (BMO), are among nine institutions named in a new US debanking report — one that found major banks had denied financial services to customers based on their political beliefs or lawful business activities.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) launched its supervisory review in September 2025 following a presidential executive order titled “Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans.”

The review examined nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 420,000 pages of documents from all nine banks — JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, and PNC Bank, alongside TD Bank and BMO — and found that all had maintained policies limiting customer access on non-financial grounds at some point between 2020 and September 2025.

Broad reputation risk policies under review

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller of the Currency in Washington, described the findings as “irrefutable evidence” that these banks had “denied, debanked and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses.”

He added: “Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate.”

The OCC found that broad, poorly defined reputation risk policies, or those lacking objective and risk-based criteria, were used to restrict client access across sectors including oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms and ammunition manufacturing, tobacco and e-cigarette distribution, detention facility operations, and digital assets.

Implications for the broker channel

The OCC’s findings carry immediate weight for Canadian mortgage brokers, for whom both TD and BMO are significant lender partners.

TD Bank, which has moved to sell approximately US$9 billion in US mortgage holdings to comply with an asset cap imposed after its US$3.1 billion anti-money laundering settlement, remains a major broker channel lender in Canada.

According to Canadian Mortgage Professional’s coverage of MortgageFest Canada, Devon Ajram, vice-president, broker services and operations at TD Bank in Toronto, disclosed that close to 50% of the customers TD gains through the broker channel are new to the bank, a measure of just how critical that channel is to the lender’s growth.

BMO, which has been growing its broker presence through its BrokerEdge platform, is also an expanding partner in the channel. Brokers with clients in energy, firearms retail, or digital assets should note that these sectors featured prominently in the OCC’s findings — and as CMP’s earlier reporting on big bank CEO outlooks found, US policy shifts at these lenders have a habit of crossing the border.

Comptroller Gould acknowledged that while some banks had begun moderating these practices, he was “not confident” these steps would be enough. The OCC has signalled it will consider further changes to its regulatory framework for the largest banks.

items.title: Multi-generational homes draw half of Canadian mortgage prospects
items.description: Affordability gaps are pushing buyers to pool resources, wait longer, and worry more at renewal
items.content: <p>Affordability gaps are pushing buyers to pool resources, wait longer, and worry more at renewal</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276043977835891.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Affordability gaps are pushing buyers to pool resources, wait longer, and worry more at renewal
items.body:
Multi-generational living is emerging as a mainstream strategy among Canadian homebuyers, with 53% of prospective buyers open to a shared-generation home, according to RBC’s 2026 Home Ownership Poll.

The survey of 1,810 Canadians aged 18 to 64, conducted between August 5 and 24 using Leger’s online panel, also found that 35% of current homeowners would sell and co-purchase with an adult child to help the next generation enter the market.

Janet Boyle, Senior Vice President of Home Equity Finance at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, said shared purchases carry more complexity than many buyers anticipate.

“Buying together isn’t just a mortgage decision,” Boyle said.

“It touches everyone’s longer-term financial plans, from future purchases and tax implications to what happens when it’s time to sell or pass the home on. Those conversations are much easier to have at the start, and getting holistic advice can make them simpler.”

Among those open to multi-generational arrangements, 34% cited housing affordability as the primary driver, 32% viewed it as a cost-management strategy, and 26% described it as necessity rather than choice.

Buying later, thinking longer term

The poll also documented a stark generational gap in homebuying timelines. Current owners purchased their first property at an average age of 29; non-owners expect to wait until 41, and half have no expected timeline at all.

That gap is reshaping what buyers want. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of first-time buyers planning to purchase within two years want a property they can stay in long term rather than one they may outgrow.

As younger Canadians increasingly question whether homeownership is achievable, getting that first purchase right carries more weight than ever.

Brad Evjen, Senior Mortgage Specialist at RBC, said buying for the long term adds financial pressure.

“Buying a home you can stay in longer usually means stretching your budget further, so the math has to work in both directions,” Evjen said.

The data reflects a shift brokers should already be making in how they approach every client conversation.

“A mortgage broker agent has to spend the time not just focused on the transaction, but working on the education piece,” Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said during MortgageFest 2026. 

“What’s the plan for the client, not just to get into the home, but what does it look like for the next three to five years?”

That long-term lens, she argued, is now the defining difference between rate agents and trusted advisers.

“As an industry, we got away from where it was about transactions and how many deals you did. Now it’s about focusing on that financial plan and strategy for that client, building that long-term financial relationship. So you look like a true expert and not just a rate agent.”

Renewal stress rises

For existing homeowners, the pressures extend to renewal. Among those renewing within two years, 51% describe the experience as nearly as stressful as buying their first home.

Rate concerns are the primary driver: 82% are worried about interest rate increases in the coming year, 60% expect renewal to strain household finances, and 42% wish they had started planning earlier.

A further 84% of respondents approaching renewal said the right advice makes all the difference. Mortgage brokers are turning the renewal conversation into one about cash flow, amortization, and long-term financial strategy.

items.title: Quebec home sales slide as inventory builds and sellers hold firm
items.description: QPAREB pointed to compounding pressures from rising fixed mortgage rates and cooling population growth
items.content: <p>QPAREB pointed to compounding pressures from rising fixed mortgage rates and cooling population growth</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276009920956958.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: QPAREB pointed to compounding pressures from rising fixed mortgage rates and cooling population growth
items.body:
Quebec’s residential real estate market posted its fourth consecutive quarterly sales decline in Q3 2026, with provincial transactions falling 7% year-over-year to 20,935, according to new data from the Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers (QPAREB).

Active listings climbed 20% to 42,408 units, but inventory still sits below historical averages across every region of the province, keeping sellers firmly in control.

Supply climbing, but balance remains distant

As QPAREB's housing forecast for 2026 anticipated, the provincial market was expected to moderate while remaining historically firm. The Q3 data confirms that direction.

“Despite the increase in supply and the fact that most areas of the province are in a period of transition, Quebec is still a long way from achieving a more balanced residential market,” said Hélène Bégin, senior economist at the QPAREB in Montreal.

“The upward trend in the number of available properties is beginning to ease shortages and provide prospective buyers with more choice.”

Despite slowing sales, prices have broadly held. The provincial median for a single-family home reached $500,000, up 2% from Q3 2025, while condominiums held flat at $400,000 and plexes surged 8% to $699,000.

Condominiums now average 58 days on market, nine days longer than a year earlier, signalling softer demand in that segment.

Regionally, the picture is mixed. Trois-Rivières and Sherbrooke each recorded 12% sales gains, while Montreal’s census metropolitan area (CMA) posted 9,265 transactions, down 12%, marking its fourth consecutive quarterly decline.

Quebec City’s inventory, despite a 27% annual increase, remains 54% below its 10-year average.

In September, Montreal CMA sales fell 11.6% to 3,082 transactions, with new listings up 7.2% to 7,494 and total inventory rising 19.9% to 21,793 units.

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

Fixed rate pressures hit first-time buyers hardest

Affordability is the sharpest headwind for those entering the market. Camille Laberge, assistant director of market analysis at the QPAREB, pointed to compounding pressures from rising fixed mortgage rates and cooling population growth.

“Affordability challenges are also discouraging some households from buying a home or condominium in several markets, especially among first-time buyers,” she said.

“Given the increase in fixed mortgage rates in the spring and again in early fall, and that the Bank of Canada’s policy interest rate could rise by the end of 2026 or, at the latest, in early 2027, housing affordability in Quebec is likely to continue to deteriorate, as median home prices are expected to remain high.”

Fixed-rate mortgages with terms of five years or longer fell to 8.8% of newly originated loans in July, the lowest level since records began in 2013, with the remaining 91.2% carrying shorter fixed terms or variable rates.

“The five-year fixed-rate mortgage, long the preferred option for Canadians, has been losing ground for several years to shorter terms and, more recently, variable-rate mortgages,” said the Canada Watch research note authored by Daren King, senior economist at National Bank of Canada in Montreal.

Laberge offered a practical signal: “More sellers are lowering their asking prices, a sign that the growing number of properties for sale is creating less competitive conditions” — an opening for brokers helping clients calibrate pricing as Quebec’s market slowly tilts toward equilibrium.

items.title: Inside the rise and rise of reverse mortgages in Canada
items.description: The one-time niche product is seeing its popularity climb. Industry executives explained why, and what brokers and their clients need to keep in mind
items.content: <p>The one-time niche product is seeing its popularity climb. Industry executives explained why, and what brokers and their clients need to keep in mind</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639275995304206814.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The one-time niche product is seeing its popularity climb. Industry executives explained why, and what brokers and their clients need to keep in mind
items.body:
The popularity of reverse mortgages has soared in Canada in recent years, and that momentum doesn’t appear to be slowing anytime soon.

Once viewed as a niche product, its uptake is increasing as a way for older homeowners to tap into home equity while remaining in place – and while it’s not a solution that should be offered without a careful appraisal of each borrower’s individual situation, industry members say its appeal is only spreading.

Pierre Martin (pictured, top centre), senior vice president of broker channel at HomeEquity Bank (HEB), told Canadian Mortgage Professional an evolution has taken place in recent years in industry perceptions of the product, evidenced by conferences such as the recent MortgageFest Canada summit in Toronto.

“In the last two years, you’ve really seen a different shift in these types of conferences,” he said. “More and more there are panels, there are presentations around reverse, and it’s becoming a real solution.”

That transformation, according to Martin, has been helped by the rising skillset of brokers. “Today, I think they’re real mortgage advisers,” he said. “They’re there to strategize with their client and figure out different solutions.”

Growing attention to the product on the broker side can be attributed in part to changing demographics across Canada.

Tracy Valko (pictured, top right), a leading broker and founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, highlighted the “very large” cohort of Canadians aged 55 or over, a share that’s only set to increase in the coming decades. “That’s going to give brokers the opportunity to look at equity-rich homeowners who are liquidity poor, and access that in a very responsible way,” she said.

Financial pressures bearing down on many Canadians are playing a role. With a significant share of mortgages renewing this year, Valko said brokers have a key opportunity to sit down with long-term clients and take stock of their full financial picture.

That means not just rate, but also debt load, cashflow, and longer-term needs. “We have a bigger responsibility, more than ever, to not just be their mortgage broker [with a] best-rate scenario – but more of that strategy, financial planning,” she said.

Christine Xu (pictured, top left), founder of Moneybroker Canada and a 26-year industry veteran, told CMP she’s witnessed the demand firsthand. She’s been running reverse mortgage seminars for clients – and each one fills within a day, an “overwhelming” level of response.

Bank of Mom and Dad a key factor behind product’s growth

One of the main reasons homeowners are turning to the product, Xu said, is as a way of navigating the affordability challenges facing their children.

The so-called “Bank of Mom and Dad” has become an increasingly prominent force in the Canadian mortgage market during the past 20 years, mainly because of the hurdles faced by younger homeowners in the face of rising home prices and downpayment requirements.

“I imagine a lot of the time, parents want to help their children,” Xu said. “Taking the reverse mortgage route is a very good option.”

Why brokers and their clients need to be cautious about reverse mortgages

But the product is not a blanket option for every client -a dn brokers need to approach it accordingly, Martin said, with a careful and comprehensive conversation before pushing ahead.

“Should it be for everyone? No,” he said. “And I think those are the questions you have to ask with the client: What is really the outcome you need? Is this really a solution that fits your needs? You want to protect them.”

That responsibility is exactly what makes the broker channel so well placed to drive the product’s growth, he said: a broker can assess the full picture of a client’s finances, their family situation, and their long-term plans before making a recommendation.

“It’s a way to continue living with dignity and their house and not be house poor,” he said. “And I honestly believe the help of brokers will increase the magnitude of this solution.”

items.body:
VANCOUVER — Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province's real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market.

The British Columbia Real Estate Association says in a release that just over 5, 250 homes were sold last month, down about 9 per cent from the same month in 2025.

Home sales were about 26 per cent lower than the 10-year average for B.C. for the month of September.

The association says sales volume for residential transactions in B.C. last month was $4.9 billion, down 11 per cent from a year ago, while the average price on the Multiple Listing Service fell 2.4 per cent to just over $924,000.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson says in a statement that the declines come after "an encouraging summer" where B.C. showed signs of recovery, but spiking oil prices have prompted speculation on whether the Bank of Canada will raise interest rates.

About 51,000 homes have been sold in B.C. so far in 2026, down about 6 per cent from the same period last year, with sales in September falling year-over-year in every region other than South Peace River and the Kootenays.

items.title: Demographic changes to shrink Canada's workforce: Bank of Canada
items.description: ‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’
items.content: <p>‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639274915805105444.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: ‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’
items.body:
Demographic changes will shrink the Canadian workforce and could push up wages in some sectors, according to an explainer from the Bank of Canada, which said an aging population and lower immigration are reducing the number of people working.

Canada's population grew by only 0.5% in 2025 – the weakest pace in more than a century, according to the bank. For most of the past 50 years, annual growth held at about 1.2%.

Why is Canada's labour supply tightening?

Canada's birth rate has been below replacement level for more than five decades, the Bank said, and immigration – which long filled that gap – has been falling since Ottawa began cutting levels in 2024.

Statistics Canada's quarterly estimates, released Sept. 23, 2026, show the population rose by 189,425 people, or about 0.5%, between July 1, 2025, and July 1, 2026, to 41,798,407. The population fell by 7,225 between Oct. 1, 2025, and Jan. 1, 2026. Alberta accounted for about 40% of the national increase over the year, while Ontario grew by less than 0.3%.

Under the 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), the target for new temporary worker arrivals is 230,000 in 2026, including 60,000 under the Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) Program. Ottawa aims to cut the temporary population to less than 5% of the total by the end of 2027, while holding permanent resident admissions at 380,000 a year and transitioning up to 33,000 temporary workers to permanent residency in 2026 and 2027.

The Bank noted that temporary workers often fill jobs in sectors with labour shortages, such as restaurants and agriculture, while highly skilled immigrants bring scarce expertise in fields such as computer engineering.

For employers that relied on these workers, the effects are visible. Some Prince Edward Island businesses are cutting staff hours and extending shifts as federal immigration cuts shrink the labour pool, while those still hiring them face heightened immigration law compliance scrutiny and audits.

Aging workforce raises retention and succession stakes

Canada's median age was about 26 in 1971 and is now above 40, according to Statistics Canada data cited by the Bank. Most baby boomers have reached retirement age, and fewer young people are entering the labour market to replace them.

The Bank said labour shortages could raise wages in some sectors, potentially feeding into inflation. Older Canadians also spend more on health care, adding demand in that sector.

For HR leaders, that means sharper competition for talent in sectors such as health care, alongside the loss of institutional knowledge as long-tenured staff retire. Succession planning becomes more pressing, though employers should tread carefully when asking older workers about their retirement plans, given the risk of age discrimination claims.

In the same speech, Macklem pointed to the role of employers as the economy adjusts to structural change. "Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future," he said.

items.title: New Barrie Condo Blends Several Strategies To Create Affordability
items.description:
While some condo developers are pivoting to purpose-built rentals or opting to build larger, more expensive units amid a sluggish condo market, one Barrie developer is harnessing modular and standardized construction techniques, alongside housing incentive programs, to bring affordability back to the condo market.

“Own a condo for less than rent” promises Sean Homes’s 405 Essa project, slated for the west side of Essa Road, just north of the Ferndale and Veterans Drive intersection in south Barrie. It’s an impressive offer, with monthly payments, including mortgage, taxes, and condo fees starting at just $1,500 for a $249,990, 375-sq.-ft pre-construction studio.

Also on offer are a range of units including lofts, one-bedrooms starting at $399,990, one-bedrooms with either lofts or dens, two-bedrooms starting at $499,990, and two-bedrooms-plus-den units. While final pricing for some unit types is yet to be finalized, Sean Homes founder Sean Mason says he’s aiming to make 70% of the units affordable and priced under $425,000.

“This is housing for someone making $24 an hour,” he says. “That's somebody who is a construction labourer, a painter, a waitress, or a cook. Not, not a chef, but a cook. That's who I'm trying to serve.”

To help keep costs down, Mason adapted Barrie’s Development Charge (DC) waiver program — originally intended for rental developments offering at least 20% affordable housing in intensification corridors — to a for-sale condo project. To secure a full city fee waiver, Mason agreed to make 20% of the building affordable; however, because roughly 70% of the building's smaller units naturally qualify for Ontario’s automatic provincial DC exemption for affordable housing, the city waiver effectively covers the remaining 30% of market-rate units. Barrie also recently slashed its DCs by 50%, further reducing the cost of the project.

“So for an investment of around $1.5 million, they're getting approximately 90 affordable, for-sale condo units in the City of Barrie,” says Mason. “When I speak with staff, they say, ‘our return on investment here is amazing.’”

The other piece of the puzzle was leveraging modular and standardized construction. The development is being built using large cross-laminated mass timber panels that can be easily installed, saving time and money. “We order the largest panels they can fit on a truck,” says Mason. “So it's affordable. Because then when you're lifting pieces up, you're only lifting one big piece instead of three different smaller pieces.” He’s also importing standardized balconies from the UK that are so efficient, Mason says they can install one every 15 minutes.

New technologies help shave even more off the development’s bottom line. Interior source heat pumps cut down on energy costs, plasma phase change hot water technology means they don't have to install a central boiler or run lines throughout the entire building, and robotic parking stackers negate the need for additional levels underground that require more materials and time to construct.

The seven-storey mixed-use development will contain 134 residential units featuring sleek, modern interiors, and retail at ground level. Amenities include a lobby coffee bar, co-working lounge, a year-round sauna and snow lounge, and weekly boxing and yoga classes in the fitness studio.

Shovels will be in the ground this winter, pending a strong sales launch at the end of October, which Mason is confident will happen. Occupancy at 405 Essa is expected in two years.

OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.

The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August.

The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion.

The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August.

The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion.

The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion.

items.title: Vancouver opens the door to convertible balconies
items.description: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items._ogDesc: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items.body:
Having a balcony is nice for people who want to enjoy some fresh air without leaving home. But what about balconies that could be closed off to shield residents from Vancouver’s rain and wind, and reduce the noise from the streets below?

A number of companies and developers are introducing the concept to the region—convertible balconies that can be temporarily enclosed or opened, usually using retractable glass panels.

Vancouver city council recently updated its design guidelines to recognize fully retractable glass balcony systems. The changes will take effect Oct. 27, according to the city.

“Balconies with glass panels that slide, fold, or stack open can still be considered outdoor space, as long as the glass can be fully opened, the balcony is not permanently heated, and it continues to function primarily as a balcony rather than an indoor room,” the City of Vancouver said in a statement.

The City also approved removing restrictions on how much balcony space can be excluded from a building’s floor area calculations, effective Oct. 27, giving developers more flexibility to include larger balconies in new apartment buildings.

“These changes make it easier to build larger balconies and clarify that retractable glass weather screens can be used without the balcony being treated as enclosed indoor space, provided the guidelines are met,” the city said.

Some B.C. developers and companies are applauding the changes, saying convertible balconies give residents more flexibility in how they use their living space and could make balconies more usable.

“[It’s a] big deal … that Vancouver has recognized, like many other municipalities,” said Michael Geller, a Vancouver-based developer, real estate consultant and retired architect. He is working with Finnish firm Lumon Group to introduce retractable glass panels for balconies to B.C. and has been advocating for the concept for years.

Other municipalities, including Burnaby, North Vancouver, Langley, West Vancouver and Victoria, have already allowed the technology, according to Geller.

“Sometimes it's nice to have the window open and get the fresh air, and sometimes it's nice to close because it's a bit cold [or it's raining], and it's also quite noisy driving along,” he said.

“It really makes the balcony much more usable.”

Vancouver-based Concord Pacific Developments Inc. is building a three-building high-rise complex in the Metrotown area that’s scheduled for completion next year. One of the selling points for the project is its large convertible balconies, according to Terry Hui, president and CEO of Concord.

An 825-square-foot two-bedroom unit at Concord Metrotown, starting at about $1 million, has more than 500 square feet of outdoor space with retractable glass panels that Hui said would significantly increase residents’ living space.

“The market really likes it,” said Hui, noting that about 85 per cent of the roughly 1,400 units have been presold.

“Families are very excited about it as well, to be able to have the kids on the outside space while the parents try to maintain their sanity inside. …We have one buyer that's excited about having his office outside because he likes fresh air.”

Not appealing to cost-sensitive buyers

The convertible balcony offers residents more flexibility, but it remains a premium feature given the costs and housing affordability challenges in Metro Vancouver, according to industry insiders.

“I think it's a great idea and it's a great use of space,” said Mike Stewart, a Vancouver-based real estate agent and blogger. “It makes the balcony useful for more days of the year.”

He said he sees the product appealing to buyers who value large balconies and are willing to pay a premium for the units, but less attractive to average buyers because of the additional cost it adds to already-expensive homes in Metro Vancouver.

“It's a premium thing because the people who are price-sensitive are primarily not buying the bigger, higher-end, nicer units with the large balconies,” said Stewart.

“For smaller balconies, it doesn't really make sense to [install the system].”

Stewart said he could see the product becoming more popular in markets where activity is stronger and prices are rising, as buyers may be more willing to pay for upgrades. That, however, is not the case in Metro Vancouver right now.

Geller said cost is one of the main challenges to wider adoption of convertible balcony systems in the region. He did not disclose the specific price of installing Lumon’s retractable glass system but said it can range from several thousand dollars to more than $10,000.

“But the cost will come down as it becomes more common,” he said.

Given the current tax and regulatory framework for property development, it can be difficult for developers to make a profit selling small, inexpensive units because of the costs involved, so many choose to offer more features to target high-end buyers, according to Stewart.

The convertible balcony feature, as well as other features such as EV chargers, could help projects stand out in a softer market and give them a competitive advantage, he added.

“The market dynamic is for the developers to offer more to win market share in a smaller market,” said Stewart.

“If [buyers] have a choice between a big balcony that isn't convertible and a big balcony that is convertible, and maybe the price difference isn't much, they probably would choose the convertible balcony.”

Geller believes the City of Vancouver’s approval will help make convertible balconies a standard feature in new housing projects over time.

“I would suggest that just like air conditioning is becoming almost standard in many good quality high-rise buildings, 10 years from now, most new apartments will have it in Vancouver because it makes a lot of sense,” he said.
