The post Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s home prices fell more than 20%, but BMO says population growth may have masked the economic pain of the housing crash.
items.body:
Canada’s housing crash is close to rivalling the early 2000s crash in the US. In contrast, Canada seems relatively unscathed, despite being a smaller economy that’s more dependent on housing. BMO’s chief economist notes the country is better positioned to avoid a financial crisis, but its pain avoidance is partly an illusion—hidden by Canada’s aggressive use of immigration.

Canadian Home Prices Are Following The US Housing Crash

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

The Canadian housing correction is following the same trajectory as the U.S., but with a different outcome. Home prices in Canada have dropped 20.5% from the early-2022 peak, compared with 26% during the U.S. bust. However, Canada avoided a comparable economic collapse—its real GDP grew at an annualized pace of 1.7% over the four years since prices started falling. That’s only slightly below the 2.0% average for this century, which is remarkable considering the country’s housing-dependent economy.

“This is arguably the most significant home price correction ever for Canada, and yet the economy has managed to avoid serious collateral damage from the deep decline,” explains BMO Chief Economist Douglas Porter.

He notes Canada has seen only one “traditional” recession in the past 35 years. That was the Global Financial Crisis, with 2020 being a very different policy-induced shutdown. He clarifies, “… it’s not as if recessions never happen, they are now just extremely rare events, and it takes a near cataclysm to cause a full-scale downturn.”

How? There’s some clear factors that helped mitigate the worst of the fallout—at least on the surface.

Stronger Borrowers And Rate Cuts Helped Contain The Fallout

The bank sees the brief period of peak home prices as one of the key differentiators. Porter notes prices surged 50% over the final two years, containing the damage to a relatively small pool. The correction is also largely contained in two provinces, leaving prices relatively unscathed for almost half the country. A substantial wealth cushion also helps limit spending cutbacks, while an aging population increasingly supports consumption through non-employment income such as pensions. In fact, seniors (aged 65+) represented over 1 in 5 (22.4%) dollars of consumption in 2025.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

The bank also notes that the finances were stronger. Mortgage qualification hurdles, like the stress test, helped minimize the volume of overextended borrowers. Rate cuts began less than a year after rates peaked, softening the normalization shock. Overall, the headline data reveals an economy that’s darn near invincible.

Skeptical that a housing-based economy could survive a US-style housing correction with so little damage? There’s a good reason—the apparent escape may have been partly an illusion, according to Porter.

Canada Avoided A Financial Crisis, But It Didn’t Avoid The Pain

Porter believes Canada avoided the financial crisis, but avoiding the pain is partly an “illusion.” The population grew at an annualized pace of 2.8% over two years to early 2024, generally faster than GDP averaged. This helped to offset—possibly more than offset—any pullback in GDP. The economy grew, but the population grew faster—meaning less economic output per person, despite headline gains.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

Measured per person, real GDP per capita fell in four of five quarters during the 2022-23 stretch, falling more than 2% peak-to-trough. Unemployment also climbed more than 2 percentage points over that period, a rare combination. Porter says this has only occurred a handful of times in the past 60 years—and only during official recessions.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

“In other words, some of Canada’s Housing Houdini may have in fact been an illusion, not unlike the original act,” says Porter.

items.description:
As the October 26 Toronto mayoral election approaches, the city’s housing and affordability crisis remains one of the most pressing issues among voters, and for good reason.

Fewer than 1 in 6 Torontonians can afford to buy a home in the city, minimum wage workers have to work 145 hours per month to afford the average asking rent for a one-bedroom apartment, and while the city pledged to facilitate 285,000 new homes by 2031 in 2022, it’s only achieved 32% of that goal as of this August.

Toronto’s top mayoral candidates — Incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow, and former urban planner and City Councillor Brad Bradford — both say they can put a good dent in Toronto’s housing and affordability woes, but they differ on how to pull it off. Here’s how Bradford and Chow plan to tackle the housing file:

Olivia Chow

City-led affordable housing

Under Chow’s lead, housing has shifted out from under the domain of the private market toward a more public, city-led development model. Since Chow took office in 2023, 5,271 city-owned housing units have broken ground, including 1,680 affordable units. Her plan is to continue building affordable and rental units via her public development model, with a goal of delivering 65,000 rent-controlled homes by 2030. She also wants to encourage development through new incentive programs that cut fees for developers in exchange for affordable units.

Cutting red tape

Chow champions zoning reforms that allow for more missing middle housing, including as-of-right multiplexes, and fast tracking transit-oriented developments. She’s also working to streamline the development review process with pre-approved building plans and expanding the online application process with automated checks and submissions. Chow has said efforts like these have made Toronto 80% faster at approving new housing. She has also eliminated development charges (DCs) for projects up to six units, created an incentive program that eliminates DCs for purpose-built rental housing, and played a central role in securing the $1.5 billion tri-governmental deal to lower DCs by 40%-60% in June.

Protecting tenants

Chow has promised a $2.15-million bad landlord task force under RentSafeTO, if re-elected. The task force would use enforcement officers and lawyers to investigate reports of neglectful landlords and buildings in disrepair. Fines paid by landlords and RentSafeTO funds would pay for the initiative.

Expanding taxes

Chow says she backs increasing taxes on vacant and luxury homes to fund affordable housing and prevent speculation. It’s a stance she has been consistent on. In 2023, she created the luxury property tax and voted to increase the vacant homes tax from 1% to 3%.

Brad Bradford

Private development

Bradford disagrees with Chow’s public builder model for delivering affordable housing, favouring partnering with experienced non-profit and market builders who he believes can build housing faster and cheaper than the City has.

Cutting red tape

As the former Chair of the Planning and Housing Committee, Bradford brought forward the Housing Action Plan to legalize gentle density, update urban design rules like eliminating the angular plane, and speed up approvals. If elected, he promises to continue updating city guidelines and streamlining the development review process, in part by increasing the use of technology. Bradford has also long called for the dropping of DCs to get shovels in the ground faster. He put forward a motion to lower DCs by 25% last March, which was rejected by Chow, and voted in favour of slashing DCs by 40% or 50% this June.

Renter strategy

Bradford is proposing a three-part plan to help renters: “Keep your home. Cool your home. Build more homes.” He wants to keep the existing renoviction by-law, but improve its enforcement by implementing a public dashboard to keep track of licenses and investigations and provide more funding for enforcement. He also wants to ensure renters have at least one cool room in their house, without any rent hikes to pay for it. Finally, Bradford promises clearer rules and earlier funding for non-profit rental builders instead of one-off negotiations for each site.

No to taxation

Bradford is against raising taxes on vacant and luxury homes, and has said he wants to keep costs down for all Torontonians. If elected, Bradford also promises to eliminate Toronto's Municipal Land Transfer Tax for homes valued at or below $1.1 million.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada Lost 110,000 Jobs Over Two Months, Wiping Out 2026 Gains

The narrative of Canada’s resilient job market has flipped in just two months. Employment fell by roughly 70,000 jobs in September, totaling a drop of 110,000 since August. The two-month slump was so sharp that it wiped out any year-to-date gains, putting 2026 in the red. Bearing the brunt of the downturn are entrepreneurs, public workers, and young adults. This seems to be an increasingly common theme in recent years.

Canadian Rents Fall For 24th Month, Driven By Shrinking Unit Size

The average rent landlords are asking fell for a 24th straight month across Canada. The average fell to $2,034/month in September, 4.2% lower than last year and 9.2% below the May 2024 peak. A breakdown reveals the data is heavily skewed by region and size. The drop in Ontario was enough to eliminate the continued surge in provinces like Nova Scotia. At the same time, more than half of the national drop can be explained by shrinking apartment sizes.

Canadians Continue Migrating To Alberta and BC, Flee Ontario

Canada’s great internal migration shows over 110,000 residents moved to a new province in Q2 2026. The biggest winner continues to be Alberta’s net gain of 5,893 residents in Q2 2026, making it the top destination. Ontario was on the losing end, with 7,063 more residents leaving than it gained from other provinces. Holding onto the bottom of the list for years now suggests Ontario’s problems are now systemic.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Home Prices Plunge To 6-Year Low, 28% Below Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto fell 0.9% to $917,600 in September, and now sit 28.3% below March 2022’s peak. Last month saw the second-weakest sales volume for September in over 15 years. Active listings also came in at the second-highest volume over the same period. The weak demand balance leaves the region in a buyer’s market, where prices are expected to fall.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Home Prices Hit A 5-Year Low As Buyers Pull Back

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver slipped 0.6% to $1.08 million in September, 5.5% lower than last year. The drop came with an 8.2% drop in sales, leaving volumes at levels rarely seen outside of a recession. Inventory tightened slightly, but remains at one of the highest September volumes. The persistently weak demand and strong inventory have pushed prices to a 5-year low.

items.title: Fraser Valley listings rise as homebuyers remain cautious
items.description: Langley was the only market in the region to record year-over-year sales growth in September
items._ogDesc: Langley was the only market in the region to record year-over-year sales growth in September
items.body:
After a quieter summer, more homes came onto the Fraser Valley market in September, but buyers remain cautious despite declining prices.

There were 2,818 new listings in the region in September, an 18.8 per cent increase from August, according to the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board’s September market report. But the total was 18.2 per cent lower than a year earlier.

Sales totalled 922 in September, down two per cent from August and 4.2 per cent compared from September 2025.

“As buyers remain cautious and sellers face greater pressure to attract attention, subdued demand continues to weigh on home prices across the Fraser Valley,” the board said.

Benchmark prices continued to decline across property types in the region. The benchmark price for a detached home stood at $1.3 million, down 1.5 per cent from August and 8.8 per cent year-over-year.

The benchmark price for an apartment fell 0.9 per cent month-over-month and 9.3 per cent year-over-year to $461,800. Townhouses had a benchmark price of $745,300, down 0.7 per cent from August and 6.2 per cent from September 2025.

“For buyers who are in a position to act, this represents a significant shift in affordability and may create an opportunity for some households to move into a different segment of the market,” said Ishaq Ismail, chair of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement Monday.

Langley and North Delta saw stronger performance than some other cities in the region. Langley had 226 sales in September, up 3.1 per cent from August and 4.1 per cent from a year earlier. New listings rose 20.7 per cent month-over-month to 583.

North Delta recorded 39 sales, a 34.4 per cent increase from August, although sales were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year. New listings increased 32.5 per cent month-over-month.

Surrey had 1,124 new listings in September, a 15.6 per cent decline from July and a 17.8 per cent decline from August 2025. Sales edged up 0.7 per cent compared with August 2025 to 404.

In Abbotsford, new listings rose 24.5 per cent from August to 365, while sales fell 21.5 per cent to 113. Compared with September 2025, new listings were down 15.7 per cent and sales declined 18.1 per cent.

Mission saw new listings jump 42.3 per cent month-over-month to 148, while sales fell 9.4 per cent to 48. Year over year, new listings declined 13.4 per cent and sales dropped 22.5 per cent.

“A succession of economic shocks have conspired to weigh on consumer confidence, keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” said Anthony Boone, interim CEO of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement.

“Despite lower prices and more choice, buyers remain cautious, and that is being reflected in the pace of sales.”

Across the Fraser Valley in September, condos took an average of 46 days to sell, while single-family detached homes took 45 days. Townhomes took an average of 38 days to sell.

items.description: More sellers returned to the market in September but not in Surrey
items._ogDesc: More sellers returned to the market in September but not in Surrey
items.body:
The red hot days of the region’s real estate scene seem like a distant memory as inventory increases and prices continue to gradually decline in the Fraser Valley.

The latest monthly market report from the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board (FVRB) notes buyers remained cautious in the region despite continued weakening prices.

September 2026 sales saw a two per cent decrease from this August, and four per cent below sales from September 2025.

After a quiet summer, more sellers returned to the market this September, with new listings up overall from August, but below the same month last year.

Overall inventory in the region remained almost unchanged in September, but still 31 per cent above the 10-year seasonal average.

However, new listings, as well as active listings, were down in Surrey last month.

“Buyers have been waiting for months for greater economic certainty,” said Anthony Boone, Interim CEO of the FVRB, in a news release.

“But a succession of economic shocks have conspired to weigh on consumer confidence, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. Despite lower prices and more choice, buyers remain cautious, and that is being reflected in the pace of sales.”

According to the FVRB, the September 2026 benchmark price for a single-detached house in the area of Surrey-Central was $1,304,100, down nine per cent from September 2025.

In September 2023, the benchmark price was $1,584,800.

The September 2026 benchmark price for a house in Surrey-Cloverdale was $1,317,200, down almost seven per cent from the same time last year.

Last month’s benchmark price for a house in Surrey-North was $1,252,600, down almost 11 per cent from September 2025.

The benchmark prices for townhouses and condos in all those areas also saw reductions over the year, with condos taking the biggest hits.

It was much the same for South Surrey/White Rock, where last month’s benchmark price for a detached house was $1,612,500, down 7.4 per cent from September 2025. That area saw townhouses take a bigger year-over-year drop (11.2 per cent) than condos (7.7 per cent).

items._ogDesc: Canada lost 110,000 jobs in two months, wiping out 2026 gains. Public sector and youth employment fell as finding work became harder.
items.body:
Canada’s job market continues to stumble, erasing any gains made year-to-date. Statistics Canada’s (StatCan) September Labour Force Survey (LFS) shows a sharp drop in employment. Public sector workers and young adults carried virtually all of the pain.

Canada Lost 110,000 Jobs In Just Two Months

Source: StatCan; Oxford Economics.

The agency reported that seasonally adjusted employment fell 0.3% (-68.3k jobs) to 21.11 million in September. This follows the 41,700 jobs lost in August, adding up to a whopping 110,000 jobs lost in the span of just two months. The abrupt decline rolls back roughly 61% of the jobs added between April and July, leaving annual employment growth just 0.5% (+94.9k jobs) higher than last year. For context, the country’s population added roughly 189.4k over the 12 months ending September 1st.

The decline surprised the market consensus that expected 10,000 jobs to be added, according to National Bank Financial (NBF). “… the renewed strength in the labour market this summer may have been overestimated,” explains NBF Deputy Chief Economist Matthieu Arseneau and Senior Economist Alexandra Ducharme.

Canada’s Job Losses Are Mostly Public Workers and Entrepreneurs

StatCan notes the public sector lost 70,000 jobs in September, its fourth consecutive drop. The monthly drop more than accounts for the loss last month, the entire sector shrinking 2.6% (-118.7k jobs) in the past year. It’s unclear what share of last month’s drop was expected, as the end of Census 2026 was expected to reduce the size of the sector.

The agency also reported a loss of 22,500 self-employed workers last month, and 24,100 private sector jobs gained. The latter was “little changed,” according to StatCan, meaning it wasn’t statistically significant relative to the sector’s size.

Education shed 35,000 jobs, despite recent total enrollment data showing growth instead of an expected contraction. Education “often shows volatility at the start of a new school year,” notes Tony Stillo, Director of Canada Economics at Oxford Economics.

Healthcare and social assistance (-23,000) represented the second largest loss of any sector. However, the sector is far from hard hit—over the past year, it added 93,000 jobs against a national gain of just 95,000. Last month’s drop was the first it has seen since December 2022.

Youth Job Losses Lead, Work Gets Harder To Find

The vast majority of jobs lost last month were held by young adults, who represented 70% of the month’s net decline. Despite the loss, the youth unemployment rate remained unchanged at 13.0% in September. That’s exactly double the national unemployment rate, which also managed to only rise by 0.1 points.

NBF notes the national unemployment rate climb was relatively small due to the participation rate, which dropped 0.2 points to 64.8% in September. The population added 23,700 people aged 15 and older, but the agency reported 52,900 fewer in the labour force.

Employer layoffs aren’t hitting as hard as media reports may suggest, but it’s harder to find a job. StatCan reported the layoff rate remained near its pre-pandemic average. At the same time, their data shows just 30.6% of those unemployed in August found a job in September. In contrast, the ratio was 32.8% a year ago, and averaged 36.5% pre-pandemic.

Both NBF and Oxford Economics warn this report shows a weaker-than-expected economy. Arseneau and Ducharme argue the Bank of Canada “needs to exercise patience before raising rates,” additionally pointing to subdued wage pressure. On the flip side, Oxford’s Stillo sees a 25 basis point rate hike in both October and December, citing fuel-driven inflation risks.

items.title: Opinion: Canada’s housing crisis needs a new approach to ownership
items.description: Building more homes matters, but affordability also depends on financing, construction costs and creating realistic pathways into ownership
items._ogDesc: Building more homes matters, but affordability also depends on financing, construction costs and creating realistic pathways into ownership
items.body:
Housing affordability will inevitably dominate the political agenda as election debates intensify. For millions of Canadians, the question is whether they will ever be able to move from paying for housing to owning it—and building more homes will not solve that problem if they cannot get through the door.

The political response has rightly focused on supply. Canada needs to build more homes, and we need to build them faster. But after decades working across development, construction and investment, I have come to believe that the housing problem is not simply a shortage of buildings. It is a system that is not working well together. The way we build, finance and access ownership have become separate conversations, when they need to be part of the same solution.

The numbers show why. According to Statistics Canada in 2023, the median renting family under 35 had just $12,000 in liquid assets. Even if that entire amount were put toward a home purchase, the median family would still have been $80,000 short of a 20 per cent down payment. For renting families aged 35 to 44, the median shortfall was $97,000.

And the ability to close that gap is becoming harder when so much income is already going toward housing. StatCan found that in the first quarter of 2024, renters spent 33.3 per cent of their income on housing, compared with 22.8 per cent for homeowners. Renters also had negative net savings of $707 on average, compared with positive net savings of $2,835 for homeowners.

The barrier to ownership is not always the ability to make a monthly housing payment. For many households, it is the capital required to get into the market in the first place. StatCan has also pointed to the growing role of family wealth and inheritance in helping younger Canadians enter the housing market, raising the risk that the ownership gap becomes even harder to close.

That is the part of the housing conversation we need to change. Canada needs to innovate on both sides of the equation: how we build homes and how people access ownership.

On the supply side, Canada cannot build at the scale we need using a system that is slow, fragmented and expensive. Modern methods of construction can improve predictability, reduce waste and shorten construction timelines. But the objective should not simply be to build faster. It should be to create a more efficient housing delivery system, so those efficiencies can ultimately translate into more attainable homes.

The same thinking needs to apply to capital. Building a home is one challenge; getting the right capital into a project at the right time is another. Even when a home gets built, the traditional financing model can leave many Canadians on the outside looking in.

We need to think more creatively about how private, institutional, and impact capital can be structured to support attainable ownership, including new approaches to the upfront capital required to get into a home. This is not about replacing the mortgage or pretending that one new financing model will solve the housing crisis. It is about recognizing that the current system was designed for a different market. If the economics of housing have changed, we need to be willing to question some of the assumptions built into how we deliver and finance it.

Municipalities have an important role to play, too. Housing is ultimately delivered in communities, and local governments understand the land, infrastructure, workforce and economic conditions that determine whether a project can actually get built. They can help accelerate housing delivery by streamlining and expediting approvals, while working with builders, investors and other private-sector partners to test new approaches and identify what can be replicated at a larger scale.

That experimentation matters because there is no single Canadian housing market. The economics of building and owning a home in Vancouver are very different from those in a smaller community on Vancouver Island or elsewhere in the country. But the underlying problem is increasingly shared: people who can carry the monthly cost of housing are finding it harder to build equity through ownership.

We should therefore broaden what we mean when we talk about affordability. It is not only the monthly payment. It is the deposit, the financing structure, the cost and speed of construction, and the time it takes to deliver a home. Ultimately, it is whether a household has a realistic path to ownership. Solving that problem requires us to stop treating construction, capital and homeownership as separate problems. They are connected parts of the same system. If we can build more efficiently, deploy capital more effectively and create practical pathways into ownership, we have a much better chance of creating housing that is not just available, but attainable.

Canada absolutely needs to build more homes. But if we want to address the affordability problem Canadians are telling us matters, we need to think beyond supply alone. We need to build a housing system that makes homes easier to build—and possible to own.

Josh Hunt is the founder and CEO of IGV Housing, an integrated housing platform making homes easier to build and possible to own.

items._ogDesc: Canadian asking rents dropped for a 24th month in September. But with units shrinking 4.2%, renters are paying less because they get less.
items.body:
Canadian rents continue to fall but a lack of demand hasn’t been the driver. Rentals.ca and Urbanation data shows asking rents fell in September. This marked a 24th straight month of declines, mostly in condo apartments. However, more than half the drop within the past two years was due to shrinking unit size.

Canadian Rents Have Dropped For 2 Years Straight

Source: Rentals.ca; Urbanation.

The average asking rent for all unit types fell for a 24th straight month to $2,034/month in September. That brings prices 4.2% lower than last year, and 9.2% (-$168) below the May 2024 peak. While last month was the weakest September since 2022, asking rents are still 16.2% higher than they were in 2021.

“According to Statistics Canada, average weekly earnings in Canada have risen by 19.4% over the past five years, indicating a general improvement in rental affordability,” explains the author of the report. However, recent Bank of Canada research shows wage gains are concentrated in older households. That’s not quite the relief suggested in the headline.

The slump is primarily in Ontario (-4.8% y/y), Manitoba (-3.2%), B.C. (-2.9%), and Alberta (-2.6%). Meanwhile, in Atlantic Canada (+3.5% y/y), where studio (0-bedroom) apartments came in a mind-boggling 34.5% higher. Inflation has also been tracking much higher on the East Coast. Clearly, rent is one of those factors.

Mom and Pop Investors Are Seeing Rents Fall Fastest

Mom and pop investors are getting a reality check. Asking rents for condo apartments fell 7.8% y/y to $2,052/month, while secondary low-rise units fell 7.4% to $2,016/month. In contrast, purpose-built units only fell 2.7% to $2,036/month over the same period.

The report didn’t dive into the reasons behind the divergence, but there are some obvious factors at play. The recent low-rate boom produced a large number of cashflow negative speculative landlords (a.k.a. speculords). They’re likely less prepared to hold out than institutions. Taxpayer-funded bailouts and loans for institutions also push the odds in their favor.

Canadian Renters Are Paying Less Because They’re Getting Less

Now for the bitter truth—landlords are asking for less because they’re providing less. The average rental unit shrank to 852 sqft in September, down 4.2% over the past two years. That explains more than half of the 7.3% drop in average asking rents over that period. A falling headline number is amplified by the shrinking apartments offered.

Falling average rents are tricky, not unlike the average income as we mentioned above. The drop is influenced more by smaller units than it’s driven by an actual correction. There’s been little progress over the past two years, and a massive disconnect still remains.

items.title: Metro Vancouver industrial vacancy falls to 2.6% while office market softens: report
items.description: New listings pushed office vacancy higher in both downtown and suburban markets
items._ogDesc: New listings pushed office vacancy higher in both downtown and suburban markets
items.body:
Metro Vancouver’s office market softened in the third quarter while the region’s industrial sector continued to tighten amid strong leasing activity and limited supply.

Office vacancy rates increased in both downtown Vancouver and suburban markets, reaching 12.2 per cent and 7.9 per cent respectively, according to Colliers’ Q3 2026 national market snapshot released Thursday.

“The office market, after 12 months of fairly solid activity and a shrinking vacancy rate, has hit a period of stabilization whereas the industrial sector is evolving,” said Susan Thompson, director of research for Western Canada at Colliers.

“It's heavily driven by logistics and the movement of goods, which is driving a lot of the activity.”

The increase of office vacancy rate came as about 350,000 square feet of negative net absorption was recorded across Metro Vancouver, largely because of new listings entering the market, particularly in Burnaby and Richmond, according to Colliers.

“Vancouver, if you’re looking at the office market, it hasn’t found the same kickstart to its industries and economies that drive activity the way a lot of the rest of Canada has,” said Thompson.

“So it’s really feeling a bit sluggish and stalled at the moment.”

Downtown Vancouver has one of its highest vacancy rates in more than 20 years, while the suburban market is performing better by comparison, according to Thompson.

Surrey’s office vacancy rate was about 7.6 per cent. Burnaby and Richmond have also seen relatively strong leasing activity, although newly completed buildings and new listings affected vacancy calculations during the quarter.

She attributed part of the difference to the composition of suburban tenants, which tend to be smaller and more stable.

Industrial market moves in opposite direction

While office conditions softened, Metro Vancouver’s industrial market continued to tighten, according to the report.

Industrial vacancy fell 0.5 percentage point quarter over quarter to 2.6 per cent, while availability declined 0.7 percentage point to 3.7 per cent.

It was the first time in 10 quarters that both vacancy was below three per cent and availability was below four per cent, according to Colliers.

“Metro Vancouver's industrial market continued to tighten this quarter as strong leasing activity, coupled with limited new availability, pushed both vacancy and availability lower,” the report said.

The region recorded nearly 1.3 million square feet of positive net absorption during the quarter, supported in part by several major lease transactions.

One of the largest was the leasing of 411,417 square feet at 18111 Blundell Road in Richmond, removing a substantial block of industrial space from the market.

The industrial market is also undergoing a broader structural shift across Canada, as demand increasingly extends beyond traditional logistics facilities toward manufacturing, advanced research and development, defence and other activities tied to Canada's emerging economic strategy, according to Colliers.

"I expect we are on the cusp of a foundational shift in Canada's industrial economy, and commercial real estate is at the heart of it," said Adam Jacobs, head of research for Colliers Canada, in a statement.

"For years, our national supply chains have been too reliant on international suppliers. Now, with historic new investment in defence and infrastructure, we are seeing the direct real estate requirements needed to bring that ambition to life."

Election uncertainty adds another layer

Thompson said uncertainty surrounding B.C.’s municipal and provincial elections is also contributing to caution among businesses making longer-term real estate decisions.

“With an election both at the municipal and provincial [level] going on across the board in B.C. right now, that’s really stalling a lot of decision-making,” she said.

She expects some of that uncertainty could ease after the elections, potentially allowing businesses to make longer-term decisions.

“We could potentially see things unlock once there’s some more certainty in what people are going to be facing,” Thompson said.

items.title: This BC Masterplan Has Buyers (Finally) Stepping Out From The Sidelines
items.description:
For the past couple of years, purchasing a home has felt like a bet very few have wanted to make. From shifting market dynamics to panic-inducing headlines, there's a slew of reasons the sidelines have been the preferred seating for would-be buyers.

Then, The Rail District by Infinity Properties in Abbotsford opened the doors to its first condo building. At The Mason, which completed this spring, 10 condos sold in a single 30-day stretch. And in the months since May, they've just kept on selling.

In a market where the broader conversation around real estate has skewed negative, a building that's actually moving (and moving fast) is worth a second look — and some questions. The first being, perhaps: Why?

"Buyers are savvy," says Ryan MacDonald, Director of Sales and Marketing at Infinity Properties. "They understand the best value may not necessarily be the lowest price."

The Mason Suite Interior (Infinity Properties)

The Mason Suite Interior (Infinity Properties)

At The Mason, this value shows up first in the floor plans: one-bedroom homes start at 643 sq. ft, larger than the market average, giving buyers "room to entertain, relax, and make the space their own." The finishes carry the same logic, with brick façade exteriors, gas ranges, gas BBQ hookups on private balconies, and extra soundproofing between floors all coming standard.

And that value extends past each unit's front door, into the surrounding neighbourhood Infinity has crafted.

The Mason sits within The Rail District's first phase, anchored by The Station — the community's amenity building — where residents across all five planned neighbourhoods can work from a shared workspace, train in the gym, or host a private gathering in the kitchen and lounge.

Just outside, the Rail Plaza does the same job at street level: timber benches and tables, room for food trucks, garden beds, and bike racks for the after-ride crowd. From there, the new Rail Trail follows the old CP Railway straight into Historic Downtown Abbotsford, linking the building to a stretch of the Fraser Valley known for its restaurants, breweries, and small businesses.

That combination — a larger home, a suite of top-tier amenities, and a neighbourhood already within reach of downtown — is shaping who's showing up to buy. The Mason has drawn a wave of first-time buyers using the GST rebate to get into the market, along with right-sizers who want the area's lifestyle without the stress of a house to maintain.

Across The Rail District more broadly, Infinity is seeing younger couples and families looking to settle somewhere walkable, with room to grow alongside the development itself.

What's notable is that last part — the masterplan is still taking shape. MacDonald reads this early appetite as a vote of confidence, rather than simply being a response to an opportune price. "Buyers will invest in a community when they are confident in its value and long-term investment security," he says. "But of course, they're also drawn to The Rail District because it's a place they can picture themselves living. It's a friendly, family atmosphere, and will continue to get better and better as the community grows."

Rail District aerial (Infinity Properties)

Infinity knows this pattern because the company has seen it before. The Mason's early momentum echoes what Infinity created at Versant, its development in Burke Mountain, Coquitlam, and the success of both is credited to the same anchoring instinct.

"The common thread is the attention to detail and pride in our work," MacDonald says. "Infinity strives to build communities that we ourselves would want to live in." In fact, several Infinity employees, he added, do live in company-built communities.

Versant (Infinity Properties)

That instinct is also what determines where Infinity chooses to bring a development to life.

"Location remains the number one factor when it comes to making a buying decision and holding its value long-term," he says. Floor plan, product quality, and a builder's reputation all matter, he affirms, but it's the community itself that a buyer lives with day to day. Infinity, he says, "will only pursue locations where we can picture ourselves."

The Rail District, evidently, is one of those locations. And with homes selling at such a robust pace since its spring launch, The Mason has already given Infinity the strongest kind of proof: buyers can picture themselves there, too.

items._ogDesc: Greater Vancouver home prices hit a 5-year low as sales weaken and unsold inventory stays elevated, pointing to further downward pressure.
items.body:
Greater Vancouver didn’t see the housing correction Toronto did, but it’s unclear if that was just a delay. Greater Vancouver REALTORS (GVREB) data shows sales fell in September. Combined with elevated inventory, weaker sales pushed prices to a 5-year low.

Greater Vancouver Home Prices Fall To A 5-Year Low

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver (composite benchmark).

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver fell 0.6% (-$6.0k) to $1.08 million in September, 5.5% (-$62.4k) lower than last year. Since peaking in 2022, prices have dropped 14.1% (-$176.9k) and sit at the lowest level since March 2021.

Greater Vancouver Home Sales Fall To Multi-Year Low, Inventory Remains Lofty

Greater Vancouver composite home sales vs active listings in September.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The region saw 1,720 existing homes sold through the MLS in September, 8.2% (-158) lower than last year. The drop marked the weakest September since 2022, which doesn’t seem that bad. However, a quick peek at historical data and it’s clear the past few years were unusually slow for Vancouver. September sales volumes this low were generally associated with recession years in the two decades prior.

On the supply side, the board reported 5,850 new listings, 10.3% lower than last year. Even with the drop, only four Septembers have seen a higher inflow in the past 20 years. This is a historically strong volume that’s fairly rare for a region that’s historically light on supply.

The demand balance suggests that prices may move lower. The CREA-preferred sales-to-new listings ratio (SNLR) was just 29% in September. That’s well below the balanced range of 40% to 60%, placing it firmly in a “buyer’s market,” where experts see prices falling further. Elevated unsold inventory may add to that pressure, with 16,390 active listings last month. While down roughly 4% from last year, it’s still the third-highest September total the board has reported in over 15 years.

items.title: Average asking rents fall 4.2% in September, marking 24 months of decreases
items.description:
The average asking price for a rental unit in September was $2,034, down 4.2 per cent compared with a year ago.  
 A monthly report from Rentals.
items._ogDesc: The average asking price for a rental unit in September was $2,034, down 4.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.
items.body:
The average asking price for a rental unit in September was $2,034, down 4.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation said the figures mark two full years of annual declines, the longest downturn the Canadian rental market has experienced in recent history.

Average asking rent prices in September were down 7.3 per cent over the past two years and 9.2 per cent below the peak of $2,202 in May 2024. The report also highlighted figures from Statistics Canada that show average weekly earnings have risen 19.4 per cent over the past five years, signifying a general improvement in rental affordability.

Rents edged slightly lower on a monthly basis, down by $1 compared with $2,035 in August, a second consecutive monthly decrease. The report said this is part of a typical seasonal pattern where demand rises in the spring and summer and begins to ease in the fall.

Across the provinces, average rents for all property segments were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year in Ontario, 2.9 per cent in B.C., 2.6 per cent in Alberta and 1.7 per cent in Quebec. In contrast, other provinces saw increases, including 1.4 per cent rises in both Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan.

On a square foot basis, average asking rents in Canada's six largest markets came in at $2.48, falling 1.5 per cent from September 2025.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.7 per cent on an annual basis to an average of $2,036 in September, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 7.8 per cent to $2,052. Rental prices for purpose-built apartments saw the smallest annual decline across all property types.

Condo rents saw the steepest declines, led by a 9.6 per cent drop in studio condo rents. Other secondary market units like houses and townhomes fell 7.4 per cent year-over-year to $2,016.

The report said rental markets in Toronto and Vancouver are showing signs of stability though after rents hit their lowest level in five years.

"Our research shows supply has been the main driver of this correction, and in key markets like Toronto and Vancouver, new supply is moving past its peak," Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand said in a news release.

"Rents in both cities have trended higher over the past six months, and annual declines have narrowed significantly as renters come off the sidelines. Where Toronto and Vancouver go, the rest of the country follows."

A few factors support an "upcoming return to positive rent growth" in those cities, the report said. This includes the fact that construction inventory has peaked, data revisions show a modest increase in populations, and both cities are relatively less exposed to tariffs across their respective labour markets.

"In the near term, more affordable rents and move-in incentives are releasing pent-up demand from delayed household formation, as higher rents in previous years led to prospective renters living with parents or roommates for longer," the report said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Expert: We Must Build A Better Trades Training System (Or Housing Will Continue To Suffer)
items.description:
Canada has finally begun to confront its housing crisis with the urgency that it so rightly deserves.

In Ontario, policy initiatives have signalled a renewed commitment to getting more homes built. Federally, there is growing recognition that increasing supply is essential to restoring affordability.

These efforts deserve praise. Policymakers have acknowledged the scale of the challenge and taken meaningful steps to address it. But there’s another reality we can’t ignore. None of these housing ambitions will be achieved unless we have the skilled workforce needed to build them.

Every housing target ultimately depends on the availability of carpenters, electricians, plumbers, bricklayers, heavy equipment operators and dozens of other skilled tradespeople. Without them, housing policies become little more than plans on paper.

That is why the findings of the recent report Are We Ready to Build Canada? A Behavioural Analysis of Canada’s Construction Talent Pipeline and Skills Training Policy should serve as a wake-up call.

The report was prepared for RESCON by Nathaniel Barr, professor of creativity and senior advisor, innovation at Sheridan College; Michael McNamara, professor of creativity and director of the Community Ideas Factory at Sheridan; and James K. Stewart, economist and a senior fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute.

The report argues that Canada's apprenticeship challenge is not primarily an economic problem. It is a design problem.

That conclusion may seem surprising at first. For years, governments have responded to labour shortages by increasing funding, promoting careers in the skilled trades and creating programs designed to attract more apprentices. Those efforts have succeeded in one important respect: registrations have increased.

The problem is that completions have not.

The report highlights a startling statistic. Apprenticeship completion rates in Canada have remained stuck at roughly 20% of registrations since 2013. In other words, four out of five people who begin the apprenticeship journey are not completing it within the current system.

Imagine a university where only one in five students graduated. Policymakers would rightly view that as a crisis requiring immediate attention. Yet in the skilled trades, this troubling reality has persisted for more than a decade.

The implications extend far beyond the apprenticeship system itself. Every apprentice who fails to complete training represents a lost opportunity to strengthen Canada's workforce. Fewer certified tradespeople mean fewer homes built, longer infrastructure timelines and reduced economic productivity.

The urgency is magnified by demographics. More than 700,000 skilled trades workers are expected to retire by 2028. In construction alone, approximately 15% of the workforce is projected to retire by 2034.

While the labour market has temporarily eased workforce pressures, policymakers should not be lulled into complacency. Many workers have already left the residential construction industry because of current market conditions. When housing demand rebounds and construction activity accelerates, the industry could find itself confronting severe labour shortages.

The traditional approach has focused heavily on recruitment. The assumption has been that if enough people enter apprenticeship programs, completion rates will take care of themselves.

But the report challenges that thinking.

Drawing on behavioural science, the authors maintain that apprenticeship systems have been designed around unrealistic assumptions about how people make decisions and navigate challenges. Policymakers have often assumed that individuals will act rationally, remain motivated, overcome obstacles independently and persist until completion.

Human behaviour rarely works that way.

People face competing demands from work and family. They become overwhelmed by complexity. They struggle with uncertainty and self-doubt. They procrastinate. They abandon plans when obstacles appear insurmountable. These are not character flaws. They are normal aspects of human behaviour.

Behavioural science examines those realities and seeks to design systems that account for them.

That insight has profound implications for apprenticeship policy.

If apprentices are struggling because application processes are unnecessarily complicated, simplify them. If critical stages of training create bottlenecks, provide targeted supports. If participants lose momentum during long training periods, develop interventions that maintain engagement. If social isolation contributes to attrition, create mentoring programs that strengthen connections and accountability.

In short, we need apprenticeship systems designed around how people actually behave, not how policymakers wish they behaved.

This does not mean funding is unimportant. Continued investments in apprenticeship programs, labour market information forecasting and skills training remain essential. And governments should continue supporting efforts to attract young Canadians into the skilled trades.

But funding alone will not solve a problem rooted in system design.

Governments need to make apprenticeship completion rates a central performance measure. Success should not be defined by how many people enter the system. It should be defined by how many emerge as certified tradespeople.

The country is about to embark on one of the most ambitious building agendas in generations. Our ability to build more homes depends on our ability to train, support and retain more skilled tradespeople.

If we want to build more homes, we must first build a better system for the people who build them.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.

items.title: Bryan Yu: B.C. housing starts rebound in August despite weak construction outlook
items.description: Weak presales, excess inventory and a slowing construction pipeline point to softer activity ahead in B.C.
items._ogDesc: Weak presales, excess inventory and a slowing construction pipeline point to softer activity ahead in B.C.
items.body:
Housing starts in B.C. jumped in August, but the increase does not indicate strength in the construction cycle as new projects remain paused due to poor market conditions, excess inventory and saturated rental markets.

Urban B.C. housing starts rose by 39 per cent to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 39,715 units, following three consecutive monthly declines. The increase was driven by a 44.6 per cent jump in multi-family starts, while single-family starts declined 1.7 per cent.

However, housing starts fluctuate from month-to-month, and the six-month moving average remained subdued. On a year-over-year basis, housing starts in urban centres fell 7.6 per cent and were down 9.7 per cent year-to-date. Both multi-family and single-family starts declined at a comparable pace during the first eight months of the year.

Within multi-family housing, the year-to-date decline was driven by a 13.6 per cent decrease in apartment starts, which account for most new housing construction in the province. In contrast, semi-detached and row housing starts increased 30.4 per cent and 0.8 per cent, respectively.

Among B.C.'s major urban markets, year-to-date, starts declined in Abbotsford-Mission (-47.7 per cent), Kelowna (-35.5 per cent), Vancouver (-6 per cent), and Victoria (-40.8 per cent). In contrast, starts increased by 41.7 per cent in Chilliwack and by 70.3 per cent in Nanaimo, while starts in Kamloops more than doubled compared with the same period last year.

Despite weaker starts, more than 84,000 units remain under construction across B.C., primarily apartments in Vancouver, reflecting earlier construction decisions and long project completion timelines. Low pre-sale sell-through and weak residential building permit activity signal slower construction ahead, raising concerns about future housing supply and affordability.

On the employment front, business-reported payroll counts in B.C. were essentially unchanged in July, edging down by 514 positions, or less than 0.1 per cent, to approximately 2.59 million. This followed a similarly modest decline of 329 positions in June. Payroll employment remained 0.7 per cent, or 19,962 positions, above its year-earlier level. Nevertheless, the recent monthly weakness points to subdued employment growth.

Excluding unclassified businesses, payroll employment declined by 1,304 positions. This measure provides the basis for the industry breakdown below. By comparison, the Labour Force Survey reported a monthly employment increase of 17,800 in July, although the two surveys measure employment differently.

Goods-producing industries lost 554 payroll positions in July, leaving employment 0.6 per cent, or 2,124 positions, below its year-earlier level at approximately 388,990.

Manufacturing posted the largest monthly decline, shedding 754 positions, and was down 1,213 positions from a year earlier. Construction employment fell by 568 positions during the month and by 436 year-over- year. In contrast, utilities added 554 positions in July and 1,090 positions over the previous 12 months.

Service-producing payroll employment declined by 750 positions in July but remained 1.3 per cent, or 29,118 positions, above its year-earlier level.

Accommodation and food services led the monthly gains, adding 870 positions and recording a fourth consecutive increase. Administrative and support, waste management and remediation services added 660 positions, reversing the previous month’s decline. Educational services recorded the largest monthly decrease, losing 803 positions, while health care and social assistance declined by 800 positions. Despite these monthly declines, health care and social assistance posted the largest year-over-year gain, at 10,376 positions, followed by educational services at 7,486 positions.

Average weekly earnings rose 0.6 per cent in July and by 4.5 per cent from a year earlier, reaching $1,356.78. The increase was robust but partly reflected the composition of hiring. The job vacancy rate remained at 3.1 per cent for a third consecutive month, corresponding to approximately 79,585 vacant positions.

Bryan Yu is chief economist at Central 1.

Greater Toronto’s real estate recovery experienced another setback last month. Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB) data shows home sales pulled back in September. Falling sales met with historically lofty inventory, helping to push home prices to a 6-year low.

Toronto Home Prices Fall To 6-Year Low

The composite benchmark price of a home across TRREB.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.9% (-$8.3k) to $917,600 in September, down 4.7% (-$45.2k) from last year. Last month marked the fourth consecutive month of declines and pushed prices 28.3% (-$362.2k) below the March 2022 peak. Toronto Sees Fewer Sales, Inventory Remains Historically High

Greater Toronto home sales vs active listings of homes for sales in September.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sales continue to slide as the recovery hits a bump. TRREB reported 5,040 sales in September, 9.0% lower than last year and the weakest volume for the month since 2023. That said, it was still the second-weakest September in over 15 years of data.

Inventory is starting to firm, though it remains historically elevated for the demand level. There were 16,500 new listings in September, 14.4% lower than last year. On its own, this volume would be consistent with historical volumes around this time of year. In the context of current demand, it’s a lot—leaving the sales-to-new listings ratio (SNLR) at 30%, where prices are expected to fall even further.

One of the reasons for the slide in new listings might be just how much inventory is kicking around. There were 26,131 active listings in September, 9.3% below last year. However, the number is still the second-most for the month going back to at least 2010. Once again, another problem amplified by demand falling to one of its weakest levels on record.

items.title: KingSett Capital Lists Two King Street East Office Towers In Downtown Toronto
items.description:
Two high-profile high-rise office towers in downtown Toronto have officially hit the market, according to a new listing that came online last week.

The first tower is 8 King Street East, a 21-storey office tower located at the northeast corner of Yonge Street and King Street East. The building was originally constructed in 1915, and is home to 155,888 sq. ft of net leasable area, 92% of which is leased with a weighted average lease term of 3.5 years.

The second tower is 18 King Street East, an 18-storey office tower located at the northwest corner of the intersection of King Street East and Victoria Street. The building was originally constructed in 1968 and is home to 238,746 sq. ft of net leasable area, 100% of which is leased with a weighted average lease term of 5.3 years.

The two Class B office buildings sit on the same block in the financial district and are separated by the narrow office building at 10 King Street East. The location provides convenient access to King Station, Union Station, as well as the PATH network.

8 and 18 King Street East in Toronto. (RBC Capital Markets Realty)

Combined, 8 and 18 King Street East total to 394,634 sq. ft of net leasable space — including some ground-level retail space — that is 96.8% leased to 88 tenants with an overall weighted average lease term of 4.6 years.

The properties are owned by private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital — through KingSett Real Estate Growth LP No. 6 — and KingSett has achieved those numbers by completing over 35 lease transactions — new leases and lease renewals — within the past 12 months, according to the listing.

The Listing

8 and 18 King Street East were both listed on an unpriced basis last week by David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, and Keith Chan of RBC Capital Markets Realty, which called it “a rare opportunity to acquire two well-located assets of scale within a market defined by tightening supply and accelerating demand for quality office space.”

The two buildings are being made available either separately or together. Notably, however, 8 King Street East is being offered on a freehold basis, while 18 King Street East is being offered on a leasehold basis, according to the listing brochure.

  • Address: 8 King Street East / 18 King Street East
  • Year Built: 1915 / 1968
  • Site Area: 0.22 acre / 0.49 acre
  • Gross Leasable Area: 155,888 sq. ft / 238,746 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 92% / 100% (Blended 96.8%)
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: RBC Capital Markets Realty (David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, Keith Chan)

“Designed by Ross and Macdonald and constructed in 1915 as the global headquarters of the Royal Bank of Canada, 8 King is among Toronto’s most architecturally significant office properties,” said RBC in its brochure. “The Vendor completed a comprehensive exterior rehabilitation at 8 King in 2021, earning the Peter Stokes Restoration Award for best practice in heritage conservation.”

Interior photos of 8 and 18 King Street East. (RBC Capital Markets Realty)

“Across the Properties, the Vendor has invested over $20MM in capital improvements since 2014, including lobby modernization, elevator recommissioning, underground garage rehabilitation at 18 King, and ongoing mechanical and roofing programs — evidencing active and disciplined asset stewardship.”

According to RBC, downtown Toronto’s office market continues to show improvement. The downtown vacancy rate is now down to 13.6% as of Q2 2026, which represents the lowest level since Q4 2022. Specific to the financial district, the vacancy rate is even lower — 11.9%.

Year-to-date net absorption of office space in the Greater Toronto Area totalled to 2.7 million sq. ft in the first half of 2026, which RBC says is the strongest first-half performance in years. Accordingly, “A sharply depleted new supply pipeline in H2 2026 reinforces the structural advantage of well-located assets such as the Properties and sets the stage for continued vacancy compression in Toronto's Financial Core.”

items.title: Two Thirds Of GTA Condos Sold For Less Than $600K In September
items.description:
Of the 1,316 condominium apartments sold across the GTA in September, 893 sold for less than $600,000. Nearly half, 594 units, sold below $500,000.

That puts 67.9% of condo sales below $600,000 and 45.1% below half a million. For buyers trying to work out whether ownership is within reach, those transactions offer a more useful starting point than the GTA's $1,006,409 average price across all housing types.

The largest single condo price band was $400,000 to $499,999, with 390 sales. Another 299 apartments sold between $500,000 and $599,999.

The table cannot tell a buyer whether a suitable two-bedroom apartment is available at that price in a particular neighbourhood. It covers the units that sold, with no adjustment for their size or location.

Prices fell faster than in the other major categories

The average condo apartment sold for $605,257 in September, down 7.7% from a year earlier, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board's Market Watch report. That was the largest average-price decline among the four major housing categories in its summary table.

Detached prices fell 5.1%, the combined townhouse category fell 4.6%, and semi-detached prices were down 0.2%.

These are changes in the averages of homes sold, so shifts in the mix of properties affect the result. They do not mean every condo lost 7.7% of its value.

Condo sales totalled 1,316, down 7.8% from September 2025. Across all housing types, GTA sales fell 9% to 5,040. The weakness extended beyond apartments, but the condo market paired falling transactions with the steepest average-price decline in that four-category comparison.

The price decline was larger outside Toronto

The City of Toronto's average condo selling price was $640,248, down 6.1% from a year earlier. In TRREB's 905 category, which covers its reporting area outside the City of Toronto, it was $533,654, down 12%.

The $106,594 gap gives a buyer willing to change location a reason to compare apartments beyond Toronto's boundary. It is a difference between the units sold in the two areas; it does not measure the saving from moving an otherwise identical apartment into the suburbs.

A lower purchase price also needs to be weighed against condominium fees and the building's finances. The report supplies selling prices, leaving the buyer to examine the obligations attached to each unit.

The cheaper 905 average coincided with a larger decline in sales. Toronto recorded 884 condo transactions, down 5.5% year-over-year. The 905 recorded 432, down 12.4%. Both areas offered lower average prices than a year earlier; neither recorded more sales.

The sales figures cannot establish why households held back. A developer counting on lower prices to lift transactions would need to look beyond September's result.

New condos have plenty of resale competition

At the end of September, 8,226 condo apartments were listed for sale across TRREB's coverage area. Of those, 5,329 were in Toronto and 2,897 were in the 905.

Dividing those month-end listings by September's sales produces ratios of 6.0 in Toronto and 6.7 in the 905. Each area had roughly six or seven apartments listed at month-end for every apartment sold during September.

Properties arrive on the market and listings expire throughout the month, so this calculation compares available stock with one month's transactions. It differs from TRREB's published inventory trend measure and cannot forecast how long a particular unit will take to sell. Buyers have a selection of existing apartments to compare before committing.

For a new condominium project, those existing apartments are part of the competition. A prospective purchaser can compare the proposed unit's price and features with nearby resales. Any premium needs a reason that matters to that purchaser, such as a better layout or a location closer to work.

September's regional price bands do not set the correct price for a new unit. A small apartment in an older building is a poor comparable for a larger unit in a different neighbourhood. The bands do show where most completed condo purchases landed, which makes them a useful check on assumptions about the budgets a project will serve.

That check needs to include the total price. A unit can look competitive on a price-per-square-foot basis and still require a budget beyond what its intended purchaser can spend. Market Watch's price-band table does not include floor area, so it cannot resolve that comparison. It shows the total prices buyers agreed to pay.

Market Watch measures resales. It does not measure condo presales, construction starts, completions or developer finances. Those require their own evidence. A new project's price has to hold up against the resale units its target purchaser can afford today.

items._ogDesc: Canadians made the largest interprovincial migration in 3 years in Q2 2026. Alberta saw massive inflows, while Ontario's exodus is structural.
items.body:
Canadians just made the largest migration across provinces in 3 years. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows 116,832 residents in Q2 2026 made an interprovincial migration, the most since 2023. The numbers reveal Alberta continues to be the top spot in the country for people looking for a new province. Meanwhile in Ontario, the mass exodus continues as residents seek better opportunities.

Alberta and BC Continue To Attract Canadians, Ontario Not So Much

Canadian interprovincial migration by province: the balance of residents that left for another province and those who arrived, Q2 2026.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadians continue to flock to Alberta, with the biggest net positive inflow in the country. The province managed to score 5,893 more residents from other provinces than it lost in Q2. It was followed by British Columbia (B.C.) with a net gain of 2,756 in the quarter. In a distant third place was Nova Scotia with a net gain of 963 residents from other provinces.

Ontario continues to hemorrhage residents with a net loss of 7,063 residents in Q2. It was followed by Manitoba (-1,847) and Quebec (-1,233). The agency’s numbers don’t tell us why or who exactly is moving in this flow, but the rapid climb in housing costs in these provinces is likely a contributor. However, B.C.’s wins are a kink in that narrative.

Alberta Leads As Top Destination From Other Provinces By A Wide Margin, Ontario’s Problems Look Structural

Canadian interprovincial migration by province: the balance of residents that left for another province and those who arrived, rolling 12-month sum Q2 2026.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Over the past year, Alberta has taken the crown as the undisputed top destination for Canadians. The province saw a net gain of 26,376 residents from other provinces, as it focuses on fostering domestic talent. In a distant second is Nova Scotia (+7,315), which has been punching above its weight in recent years. However, its net gain in Q2 2026 was roughly 47.2% lower than last year, pointing to a sharp deceleration as outflows rise and inflows slow. New Brunswick (+5,121) rounds out the top 3 for the largest net gains over the 12-month period.

Ontario remains the undisputed champion when it comes to losses, with a net loss of 29,713 residents to other provinces. The problem is starting to look structural, as it prioritizes immigration-based growth instead of domestic retention. For context, that loss is more than 3x the net outflows in Quebec (-8,058) and 9x that of Manitoba (-3,175) over the same period. That’s not a quarterly blip, it should be considered a hair-on-fire problem.

These losses aren’t just a shuffle, these are residents familiar with what a province has to offer—or not. It’s a window into the state of the region and the opportunities it presents. Policymakers are unlikely to notice the losses over the short-term, as immigration more than covers the headline outflows. But it’s not as easy as it may seem to fill the talent gap over the medium term—or retain the highest quality immigrants, who are also likely to flow where the opportunity is presented.

items.title: Toronto Rolls Out Free Pre-Approved Plans For Fourplexes, Sixplexes
items.description:
Toronto property owners looking to add homes to their lots can now start from a set of drawings the City is offering for free.

The City has announced four multiplex designs for its Pre-Approved Building Plans Program, which already offered plans for garden and laneway suites. The new plans include two fourplexes and two sixplexes, each drawn for either a narrow or a wide lot.

LGA Architectural Partners won the City's RFP to design them, with accessibility, climate resilience, cost and ease of construction among the stated priorities.

According to the City, the program lines up with Toronto's expanded multiplex zoning permissions. A fourplex is allowed anywhere in the city today, while sixplex permissions depend on where the property is located. An owner whose multiplex fits the zoning rules can go straight to a building permit application, with no stop at the Committee of Adjustment.

The pre-approval covers the building as designed. The City has confirmed each one meets the Ontario Building Code and the zoning rules that govern its design. Where it sits on a particular lot, and anything else specific to that site, will be reviewed on submission of the permit application.

Narrow Fourplex (City of Toronto)

Wide Sixplex - Side View (City of Toronto)

In terms of process, owners aren't required to submit the pre-approved drawing to get things rolling — they should enter the plan number on the Application to Construct or Demolish form, and reference their chosen HVAC type in the application; the fourplexes come in electric, gas and hybrid versions, and the sixplexes in electric and hybrid.

Site-specific work — mechanical, HVAC and plumbing, and architectural and structural components — falls to qualified design professionals, details of which the City will require in writing. Any modification, including to HVAC or plumbing, voids the plan's pre-approved status, and the owner can apply through the City's regular permit process instead.

The plans can be downloaded at toronto.ca/PreApprovedPlans.

items._ogDesc: This Week’s Top Stories include Canadian Home Prices Rolling Back To 2016 Levels, and Rents Surged Before Population Growth.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Home Prices Back To 2016 Levels After Inflation, Still Out of Reach

Canadian home prices rose—just not in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. BIS data shows home prices in Canada rose 0.78% in Q2 2026, the first increase in a year—though they remain 19.5% below peak. When adjusted to real terms, they slipped again and have fallen nearly 30% since the peak. Home prices are back to 2016 levels after inflation, but affordability isn’t.

Canadian Rents Surged 20%, But the BoC Can’t Explain How It Started

A new Bank of Canada (BoC) study shows asking rents surged over 20% between Q4 2021 and Q4 2026. The researcher shows that population growth and financing explain most growth over the period. What remains a mystery is the year-over-year surge in rents in early 2020, before the pandemic. Most of this growth is “unexplained,” according to the report. This leaves the question: Did a speculative rental bubble drive policymakers to adopt aggressive population growth?

Canada’s International Student Drop Offset By Domestic Surge

Domestic postsecondary enrollment surged in Canada, offsetting declines in foreign students. StatCan data shows total postsecondary enrollment grew 0.14% (+3.2k) to a record 2.35 million in the 2024/25 school year. A breakdown shows international students fell 6.9% (-39.6k) after the recent policy changes. However, domestic enrollment saw growth hit a 14-year high, offsetting the drop.

Canadian GDP Stalls, But Revisions Add 1 In 10 Dollars of 2026 Growth

Canadian GDP was flat in July, but the economy got bigger anyway after revisions. StatCan revisions added 0.1% more than reported growth in 2026. The revision is within the agency’s normal tolerance range, and only worth mentioning due to the slow recent growth reported. The revisions represent roughly 1 in 10 dollars added to GDP year to date.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Skyrocketed 96% As Bank Portfolios Shrink

Canadian banks continue to see mortgage borrowers fall behind on payments. Mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points in a year and the highest level since May 2014. At the same time, banks saw the number of mortgages on their books fall to 4.91 million in July, marking a 6-year low. Credit use is rising, fewer accounts are driving the growth, and more are buckling under the loads.
